utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, so you know the position, you have, we've decided, 40 minutes more, up to 40 minutes more. You don't have to take all that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Milosevic: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Golubovic, I've taken a look at your statements, both of them, and we're dealing with comments to the text in the Timok newspaper and the conversation between you and Mr. Djordjevic that you mentioned yesterday. You did talk about that text and how he commented it, I believe. However, in your statement given to The Hague investigators, on page 5, paragraph 2, you state that -- the following: "I don't remember whether I talked to Djordjevic about these comments and article." Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't say that I -- I said that I didn't remember the date and time, but I did say that we had a conversation - started by him or myself, I can't remember - and that we did comment, and I said that it wasn't in order that something like that had appeared in the press, something along those lines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, as you say, "I don't remember whether I talked about this publication," I took that to mean that you don't know whether you discussed the publication at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, again, I must interrupt. You must be fair to the witness if you're putting things from his statement. It says: "I can't remember if I spoke with the general about this publication. It's possible that I did." That's how the English reads.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. That's the point I wish to clear up, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when did you talk to him? Can you remember what year that was?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was in the year 2000, mid-2000 or the beginning of the year, thereabouts. I'm not quite sure when the article appeared, but I assume that that was round about that time. I don't read the Krimi Review, the newspaper in question, so that somebody happened to mention it to me, and that's why I said I couldn't remember exactly when all this was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, in the statement given to the working group, if it has been correctly interpreted, in paragraph 3 you state that you wouldn't have known that the event took place on the 6th of April had the newspapers not written about it and informed the public. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I can't remember the exact date, had it not appeared in the papers and had they not said that this took place on the 6th of April. I knew that it did take place at the beginning of April, but I can't give you the exact date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Now, were you at that spot near Tekija where the refrigerator truck was found on the 5th, 6th or 7th of April, 1999?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, through my recollections later, and when I checked this out, it was the 6th of April exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were at this spot near Tekija?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't at the scene of the actual occurrence, but I was in Tekija and then Kladovo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But I'm interested in whether you were at the actual scene, on the spot.

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't go out on location.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you didn't see the actual contents of the refrigerator truck.

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, neither the refrigerator truck or the contents or what went on there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I then take it that all the information you received about the refrigerator truck you received either via telephone or in direct contact with the individuals who went out on location to the spot itself?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this is not what you yourself saw, but you base what you know on the information given to you by your employees at the secretariat; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So neither you didn't count the bodies yourself later on. Did you ever see any body at all?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. You didn't see a body. Now, did you -- were you present when they transferred any of the bodies into the two trucks that were mentioned?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see, afterwards, any of these trucks going into the Batajnica centre?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you in Batajnica at all at that particular time, at the material time, for you to be able to see any events linked to that occurrence?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was never there, then or afterwards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do you know if someone was there, do you have any information and knowledge as to who buried the bodies and where those bodies are located?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you learn at all whether any of the bodies who were -- which were counted there allegedly and transported, whether they turned up and were found anywhere at all?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. All I know was what the papers published later on and what I read in the papers, but I personally know nothing about that, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who told you and how were you able to conclude that some of the bodies were wearing pantaloons, or the shalwara type of pants?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I just conveyed what I was told by the people who saw this themselves directly when the refrigerator truck was opened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Now, in the statement you gave to the working group, on page 1, paragraph 2, you enumerate the names that were -- of people who were present at the meeting, and as you say, the meeting was held at the interior affairs department in Kladovo on April 6th. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that occasion, you didn't mention that the meeting was attended by the municipal investigating judge and the public prosecutor from Kladovo. Why did you fail to mention that? Because they were there, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were there, and I mentioned this in the statement, and in other statements, that I came from Bor and found them there in the office. It wasn't an official meeting of any kind that had been convened. I assumed that they had come back from the location, from the scene itself, and were sitting there when I came in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, I understand. So you told this to the working group, but the working group failed to enter it into the note. Is that what I'm able to conclude from what you're saying now?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I saw this Official Note for the first time quite recently, when I had my first talks. Up until then, I never saw it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you happen to see the Official Note?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw the Official Note, I think, during the first conversations that I had in the offices of The Hague Tribunal. That's when they showed it to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was that, actually?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that was after the testimony of Mr. Karleusa and the technician from Kladovo, after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you saw an Official Note that was drawn up with you only after Karleusa's testimony; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you remember the names of the municipal investigating judge and public prosecutor from Kladovo who attended the meeting?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't remember the names then, and I don't remember the names now. I wasn't very interested in what their names were because I had very little contact with them. Perhaps I had seen them once or twice a few years back, but I can't say for sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. In the statement that you gave to the investigators, on page 2, paragraph 4, you state that the two of them attended the start of the investigation that took place on the spot, but that they didn't want to launch an official investigation because it was an act, as I understand it, for which the district level of jurisdiction was in charge, and that they informed the district investigating judge and public prosecutor. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what they said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I assume that you can tell me the name of the district investigating judge and prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The prosecutor, district prosecutor's name was Krsta Majstorovic, and the district investigating judge is, at the present, that is today, I think he is the public prosecutor. I don't know his name exactly, but he did appear later on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The public prosecutor, is he now the deputy district prosecutor at the time? Which of the two was it?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The investigating judge at the time is now the public prosecutor, on maybe I've got it mixed up. I didn't actually inquire, but I know that the prosecutor was Krsta Majstorovic, and I'm not sure who the investigating judge was, what his name was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether on that occasion the district public prosecutor launched a request for an investigation to be conducted into the case?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I didn't contact them, I didn't speak to them, I didn't hear them with reference to the case, and I didn't have any need to do this for any subsequent cases, because there were other services in charge of this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you actually don't know whether he launched a request for an investigation to be conducted or not.

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me now, please: From this Kladovo police station, the local police station on the territory of which this event took place, whether any minutes were taken on the investigation and on-site investigation that took place, by a crime technician or anybody else, any official information, I mean, about what took place near Tekija, what was found. Did anybody draw up minutes of what actually took place on the spot?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I wasn't informed. But I don't think so. I don't think any written report was compiled of any kind on that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm now going to ask you a question which has to do with some occurrences, some things that happened in that area along the Danube. I ask this question -- I asked the other two witnesses this question, and they gave me their answers with respect to what I asked. Two witnesses to my question said they knew about the fact that people were smuggled across the Danube. Do you know this smuggling of humans, of people, across the Danube while you were the head of the secretariat for internal affairs in Bor? Were you apprised of that?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because in that region there was a channel via which people were smuggled over. I think they were Kurds and others, and they were taken off towards Romania. And in Djerdap, this belt there, there was a channel for this kind of contraband.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the people who were citizens of our country and who were involved in this human smuggling, smuggling of humans?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that there was an individual from Tekija who did this kind of work. I know that this was mentioned in conversations, not only then but before that as well, a name was bandied about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not talking about this particular event, I was talking about the whole phenomenon.

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A man was mentioned in this connection, and I think he smuggled the people across in a boat. I don't know anything more, but it was linked to these illegal transports.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Let's move on. You say that you watched the testimony of Bosko Radojkovic, the crime technician, on television, and that he made an incorrect statement when he said that you ordered him not to take any pictures, not to take any photographs.

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's quite right. When I was in Kladovo, I didn't see Bosko, nor did I give him orders of any kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That means that he was lying when he said here that you forbid him to take any photographs?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's a matter of comment. We'll have to deal with that. It's not for the witness or for you. You can comment on it, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, you've just repeated what you said in your statement, that you had never even seen Radojkovic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, not that evening. I didn't see him that evening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you never issued an order of that kind to anybody, even to his superiors; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's quite right, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I therefore take it and conclude that Radojkovic, at his own initiative, for reasons known only to himself, failed to carry out the basic duties of a crime technician?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you cannot put what Mr. Radojkovic may or may not have thought for his own reasons, but you can ask the witness what the duties of a crime technician were.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the witness is the head of the police in that region, and linked to that function of his, he is well aware of the tasks to be completed, and duties. Now, if Radojkovic did not perform these duties, did he infringe upon his work obligations and duties, judging by the standards upheld by the witness? Is this a serious omission? As far as I understand it, this is a serious omission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Did a crime technician -- Mr. Golubovic, you can help us to this extent: Should a crime technician have taken photographs at the scene?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the investigation had been started on the spot, he would have had to have taken photographs and photographed the pulling out of the truck from the Danube and all the rest of it, everything that followed, and to follow the orders of the investigating judge. So the on-spot investigation is conducted following orders issued by the investigating judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, tell me: Did you ever ask him whether he has any photographs of the bodies from the refrigerator truck and whether you ever asked any of his superiors whether there is a photographic file and photo spread of these alleged bodies?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, quite simply, and I've already said this, that because of -- I was called away for -- on other duties, and also I wasn't directly involved in this case. It was all conducted by other services and other persons in the service and in the secretariat who were in charge of that. I just spent that night there in order to become better informed and to convey the orders and to complete the assignment I was given.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And according to your knowledge, up until this day, from what spot and in what way did the refrigerator truck come to be in the Danube? Did you ever learn about that?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The crime department or the investigating judge, did they ever happen to find and photograph any material evidence which would indicate the area from which and how the refrigerator truck came to be in the Danube in the first place?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At least as far as I know, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that from these statements of the witnesses given to the working group, to this particular working group, the one that talked to you, which through Karleusa's testimony has been introduced into evidence as exhibits, we are not able to conclude in what way and from what place the refrigerator truck came to be into the Danube?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't able to read through any of the testimonies and statements of other witnesses, and that is why I said that the Official Note in connection with talks with me I saw for the first time on that occasion. So I really don't know. All I can do is assume that Kladovo took steps to ascertain and see the place from which the refrigerator truck slid into the Danube. But there was never any concrete proof and evidence of this, anything of that kind at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Now, you say that on the 6th of April, from the local police station in Kladovo, you had a telephone conversation with the head of this particular department, Vlastimir Djordjevic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on page 3 of the statement you gave to the investigators, you say that you informed him on that occasion about everything you learnt and that you personally didn't visit the location and spot, that you didn't see the refrigerator truck or the bodies. Is that right? And in the statement that you gave to the members of the working group, you note that Djordjevic, when he rang you up after a certain amount of time, told you that an autopsy should be conducted of the corpses found.

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I said yesterday to the Prosecutor as well that that was the first time that this was mentioned during the conversation from Tekija, but not in that first conversation, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he ask you that an autopsy be conducted?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the conversation that we had at about midnight, half past 11.00 or 12.00, midnight, I asked that this should be done, and he told me that the vehicles should be dispatched towards Belgrade and that that would be conducted there, because you didn't have the resources.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you insisted that you didn't have the resources to carry out the post-mortem, but that was your reaction to his demand that an autopsy be carried out on the spot?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember, but I think that it was I myself who brought up the question of an autopsy first, and in this second conversation from Tekija, he accepted. But in the conversation from Kladovo, this was not mentioned. This was not brought up, either by me, when I informed him to begin with, or from him. Neither of us mentioned it on that first occasion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that in a later telephone conversation you asked that a truck be sent from the ministry for purposes of transport?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in that last conversation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was linked up to the further treatment and processing?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of the bodies. But it was only then that the people who were working, who were doing the job found that there were more bodies than was first stated and first assumed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So from there, we would be able to conclude that the bodies were taken in towards Belgrade because there were not the necessary facilities and resources to conduct technical analyses, identification, and autopsies on the spot at your location; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to inform Djordjevic on that particular evening about the information you had gathered as to the possible time of death of these individuals, the bodies? Did you discuss that?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because none of that was conducted. An investigation and examination of that kind was not conducted, so all that could have been done was the free assessment of the people that saw them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did I understand you correctly to say that you were not able to give him any more precise information as to the number of bodies either?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not. That's right. Not on that particular night, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So all in all, at that time, you did not have the possibility of providing any more detailed information about the bodies and about what was found in the refrigerator truck.

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't have the right information.

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't have the exact number of bodies or anything else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Why, then, did you tell him, as you said, that they were Albanians when you were not able to actually know this?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said that that was the information I was given from the people who saw the bodies, who saw the corpses, and that's what I conveyed to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But this was not a definite conclusion, in view of the fact that not all the official tasks had been undertaken or completed. This was not -- this work was not done professionally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But judging by what it said on the truck and the clothes that were found on the bodies, you said that you assumed they were ethnic Albanians. Is that what your subordinates informed you about?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that Toma Miladinovic told the working group of the Serbian MUP - and this is page K226056 in the Prosecution material - that he saw that the bodies were naked?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I said that I never received a report of any kind or read a report of any kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that Vukasin Sperlic told the working group the following: "I was personally on the spot. I don't remember anything special that was written up on the truck." He repeated that. I don't want to read the numbers of the pages he said that on to you, but that is all contained in the Prosecution material that we have for this case. All right. So you don't know that either. And do you know that Milan Stevanovic gave a statement to the working group, saying: "I noticed bodies that had clothes on, and that did not have clothes on. Then Bosko Radojkovic said to me that this is a refrigerator truck from Prizren. I know that the technician painted the inscription on the truck over." Do you know anything about these statements?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know anything about these statements.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But on the basis of these - how should I put it? - these scarce bits of information that evening, you said that the assumption was that these were Albanians. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and that is the information I sent further on to the ministry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Only on the basis of the fact that somebody told you that it says "Prizren" on the truck and they saw women's pantaloons?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and that's what I told the general.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Branislav Mitrovic said to the working group: "I cannot remember the inscription on the truck. I heard that the corpses were naked."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You've put that, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And do you know that Zivadin Djordjevic, the diver, gave a statement to the working group saying at that time there were no indications that these were corpses of persons from Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm not aware of any statements. I mean, they were never shown to me. Not a single statement was shown to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Who said to you -- because you say that you told Djordjevic that there were signs of slaughter on the corpses. That's what you say in your statement to the working group; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I said anything like that, because that evening I did not have this information except for the fact that it was said at that meeting that there had been an inscription on the truck of some company from Prizren, that women's corpses had pantaloons on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what it says here is something that you did not say?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not convey that to the general, that's for sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Because other witnesses said also that the injuries were due to a blunt object. Only one said that there was only one visible wound from a firearm. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know about that. I didn't see this on television when I watched the testimonies from here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the information about slaughtering does not come from you?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Nor from your statement given to the working group?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that moment when I was there, that could not have been ascertained, and this was not said to me either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps later, the next day, when they continued working, perhaps then. But on --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sperlic was in charge the getting the truck away?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Usually it's head of the department who is supposed to organise this kind of thing and to get it done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As for the instruction given by Djordjevic to destroy the refrigerator truck about which you speak on one of these pages, not to read all of this to you now, did you take this as a regular sanitary preventive measure in order to prevent disease from spreading? Did you interpret it that way?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that moment, Mr. Milosevic, to tell you the truth, I did have no interpretation, and this was an event that took me by surprise, like everyone else. And we all did that in relation to the orders that were issued. Probably things had to be done in a hurry because of the stench coming from the corpses. That is what I was told, that that night there was a stench already. So of course it was for preventing disease as well, I assume, that this was done, due to the sanitary conditions and circumstances.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. That's what it says here, on page 03048361, in the second paragraph, that you interpreted that as a regular sanitary preventive measure. Why did you not tell the working group? Perhaps you did tell them and they did not register it.

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You can't remember?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not all of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please explain this to me, because I have only five or six minutes left, and I have a few more questions left. And when you gave your statement to the investigators of this institution here, did you give your statement in the following way: By telling them your story continuously, or were questions put to you and did you then give your answers?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The statement was made on the basis of some questions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, so they did put questions to you and you gave answers to them?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Questions related to the event itself, and that is why I said that that was the first time that I saw this Official Note. And these questions more or less followed the course of the Official Note. I don't know if you understand what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I do understand. Let me put a very concrete question to you now in relation to this event, that is to say, the destruction of the refrigerator truck. Now when they asked you here, in order to put together this statement of yours, can you remember in which way the question was put to you? Was the question put to you as follows: Did General Djordjevic order you to destroy the refrigerator truck or why did you order the refrigerator truck to be destroyed and who ordered you to do that? How was the question put?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The question was put as follows: When did General Djordjevic, and in which sense, order me to destroy the truck, and during which conversation? I said that I do not remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, so they already assume that he was the one who gave you the order and then they just asked you when he gave the order?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now I can't really interpret that, the course of this interview.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. All right. You understand what leading questions are and what leading questions are not, because you're a policeman. Do you know Dragan Vitomirovic, the publisher and private owner of the Timok Crime Review?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long has he been doing this?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think for about ten years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did he do before he started publishing the paper?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was employed by the Ministry of the Interior, and I think that, due to certain criminal acts and also disciplinary infractions, he was dismissed from service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, so he was dismissed from the service because of crimes that he committed?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I don't know. He worked in a different department, so I'm not sure exactly what happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Did you or anybody else find out exactly where the corpses from the refrigerator truck were?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it possible - I'm asking you now about your position - that the entire event has to do with the smuggling of people across the Danube, and was used by the puppet regime in Belgrade, in cooperation with this institution, for supporting this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. That's not a question for the witness. You made that sort of speech before. It will be a matter for us to consider. Have you any more questions for him?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I have only one question, which has to do with clarifying two identical statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One is contained in this note of the working group, and the second one is in your very own statement. But the things said are identical. I'm going to quote this to you. I'm going to quote the entire sentence: "General Djordjevic did not tell me who he had consulted, but I have the impression that he talked to the minister." That is the note of the working group. And in this statement that you gave to this institution here, on the last page - again I'm quoting this to you: "I do not know whether General Djordjevic consulted the Minister of the Interior, who was Vlajko Stojilkovic at the time, or whether he consulted or informed anybody else about this event concerning the truck before he issued instructions to me." So in both places you say you do not know whether he consulted the minister, and yesterday you said that he said to you that he had consulted the minister. Why did you change your statement, both the one you gave to the working group and this institution here, in relation to this?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to explain this. At that moment when I talked to the working group, although, objectively speaking, there were not that many reasons for that, but when I had this talk at this office in Belgrade, I was not free of these official secrets, of keeping these official secrets. No official decision had been passed with regard to that. So I did not explain the structure of the organisation of the police to the investigators then, its functioning, especially in these conditions, and then I avoided telling the name. But I gave a solemn declaration too, that it is certain that General Djordjevic, during the first conversation -- or rather, the second conversation in Kladovo, that he did invoke the minister, stating that that is what should be done. So I did not mention the chain of command, any other persons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: According to the chain of command, Djordjevic is your immediate superior.

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I did not name any persons who are his. Now, that was the only reason.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever talk to Minister Stojilkovic?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know him personally?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did know him from the meetings he held with us, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as for these meetings that he held, could you come to the conclusion that he issued assignments according to the areas in which people were involved, that he never interfered in particular cases or immediate investigations?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. In regular times, that's the way it was. He did not interfere. He most probably never issued an order to me. I always got my assignments through the head of the section.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. All right, Mr. Golubovic. Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, there are no questions for Witness Golubovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, just two matters. Re-examined by Mr. Shin:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Golubovic, you had stated in your testimony yesterday that General Djordjevic had given you an instruction by telephone that the information about the refrigerator truck matter was not to be released and that none of you in that meeting at the Kladovo police station were to give any statements to the press or to the TV. Was this something that you personally informed Bosko Radojkovic about, or would someone else have informed him of that?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not understand the question. In what sense did I inform Bosko?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Actually, I'm sorry, that is my question. The instruction from General Djordjevic that the information regarding the refrigerator truck was not to be released, was that something that you had told Mr. Radojkovic personally?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not see Mr. Radojkovic. I did not contact him. I did not give him any instructions or orders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did Mr. Radojkovic work for the Kladovo police station?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So would he have received instructions from Mr. Sperlic, who was the chief of the Kladovo police station, during the course of that evening?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could he also have received instructions from Mr. Miladinovic, who is the head of the crime police in the SUP at Bor?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, professional instructions, things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And one other matter. The accused has asked you some questions regarding your -- the working group notes in which -- in particular, regarding whether General Djordjevic had consulted the Minister of Internal Affairs or not in regards to the instructions that he gave about the refrigerator truck. You had explained why you would not have mentioned that to the working group, and basically that has to do with your obligation for withholding certain secrets. Is that the same reason or is there another reason why you did not mention that General Djordjevic had received his instructions from Minister Stojilkovic when you spoke to the investigators of the Office of the Prosecutor here -- I'm sorry, Office of the Prosecutor from The Hague Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in Belgrade, when I spoke there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. But just to clarify, that was the same reason why you did not tell them that the instructions came from the Minister of Internal Affairs?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say that General Djordjevic mentioned the minister when he gave these instructions to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, that's exactly what I'm getting at. And the reason for that is the same as the reason that you didn't provide that information to the working group headed by Mr. Karleusa; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately that is the reason. That is why I stated to that group that I assumed that he had consulted someone, the minister or someone else. They asked me what I thought about that, and then I said it is my assumption that he had had consultations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And approximately when did you receive notification that you would be released from these certain secrets -- I'm sorry, this obligation to maintain certain secrets?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think when I was in Belgrade, at the office of The Hague Tribunal, that day. No. No. That day, from the Ministry of Justice, I received information that I was duty-bound, et cetera, et cetera, to respond to the summons to testify. As for the decision of the government, I personally did not receive it, except that through the media it was made public. I think that this was just before I came here, about a week before I came, that's when it was made public.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So would that have been after you spoke to investigators from the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Golubovic, that concludes your testimony. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it. You are now free to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before I call the next witness, it's probably helpful if I tidy up a few administrative matters, for fear of overlooking them. One, I suppose, technically ought to be dealt with in closed session, since the topic was touched on earlier in a closed session. It will only take a minute, but I probably ought to deal with it in closed session, with your leave.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're now in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, two exhibit matters. On the 26th of August, Exhibit 286 was marked for identification, being a list of the names of people killed in Izbica and produced in the evidence of Sadik Xhemajli. At that time, we only had a B/C/S version of the document, which is why it was marked for identification. We now have an English translation and would ask that either it forms part of 286 or becomes 286A, if the usher would be so good, and the documents become formally exhibited.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be formally marked Prosecutor's Exhibit 286A.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Also in the evidence of Sadik Xhemajli, as the Chamber may recall, the witness showed his pocketbook with handwritten notes, including notes, or rather lists, of those he alleged had been killed in the course of the incidents he described. The Chamber directed that the relevant parts of that book should be copied. That was done, and copies were distributed to the accused and to the amici and to the Court earlier this week. Translations of those photocopied and distributed pages are now available. May those be circulated, please. The original -- I beg your pardon -- the number allocated was 288, I think.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be marked Prosecutor's Exhibit 288A.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The third matter at this stage, although others may arise later, probably tomorrow, is the witness statement of the witness Antonic-Simic. The statement was obtained, it has been, I think, now circulated to the accused and to the amici. It hasn't yet been made available to the Chamber, although it should be, as supporting material for the application made and already granted. It's obviously important that the accused has it before -- and has had an opportunity to consider it before he comes to cross-examine the witness Stijovic. The final decision on calling Antonic-Simic has yet to be made. It may, for example, be a witness who we would, in the technical language of our own -- or the jurisdiction with which Your Honour and I are certainly more familiar, it may be a witness we would tender, but certainly the statement should be available to him. That brings me to the order of witnesses. In an ideal world, we would have called Mr. Coo before calling General de la Billiere, but travel arrangements and other administrative difficulties mean we're going to have to call the general first and Mr. Coo later, and I shall take the general indeed quite shortly, very shortly. My forecast of evidence is as follows: That it will be General de la Billiere, Stijovic, and then Mr. Coo, with K41, taking the position he has to take by reason of the technical arrangements that have been made for his evidence, tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's just pause there and deal with that. He will be heard by videolink tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Have we a time for that yet?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 9.00. Now, his evidence may take a little time, and one knows that the videolinks are not perfect bits of equipment. They are prone to intermittent failure. It therefore would probably be undesirable to put back the start of his evidence too much beyond 9.00 in the morning, although if there was just a little bit of evidence outstanding, it might be preferable to take that and then to take him, but we'll start with him pretty early tomorrow morning. And I would ask that, in the awful vernacular we've developed in this trial, that whatever evidence is going on this afternoon is wrapped around K41's evidence, unless there's only a little bit of it outstanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You're going to call the general now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There may be cross-examination, of course. In fact, there will be. Were you intending to call anybody else after the general?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly. If the general is finished today, I would call or certainly start Stijovic. He's here, his statement has been served, and he's ready to go. But we can wrap the evidence of whoever is outstanding at the end of the day around K41.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If you go on then. So that's K41, you've got Mr. Stijovic. Who else have you got?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Afterwards, you mean?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Oh, afterwards it's only probably Coo, Zdrilic, and then there's the little outstanding issue that you have yet to decide about, the case officer, as it were. And there may be the one other, I think, for whom there is an outstanding application, but probably not. So my calculation remains, as it has been for several days, that we're on target if we sit continuously, to finish by about Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let me deal with one matter about the witnesses. We have yet to deal with the witness about whom you made an application the other day, renewed application, and we'll give you our answer about that when we've considered it. We will give you leave to call Helge Brunborg, although that will be, as I understand it, after the adjournment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. We're grateful to you for that, that's very helpful. I'm sorry that in the event there was a misunderstanding -- there it is. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: General de la Billiere. If the witness could be brought in. I trust that the Chamber has not only had an opportunity to read his report but to at least see, without necessarily looking at, a slim file of exhibits which has been distributed to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, yes?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did I understand this correctly: There will be no changes in this witness list except for the fact that Coo may come before K41? Did I understand that correctly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. K41 is tomorrow, tomorrow morning. That's the only change there will be, if necessary. Coo comes after.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. So there are no other changes on the witness list except for Kevin Curtis, whom you've rejected altogether.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're considering him. Now, let's get on with the evidence now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just another question: Antonic-Simic Olivera. We've just received this now. She is also on the list. Will we hear her after the break or before the break? And what about this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The Prosecution, you've just heard, are considering her position. The statement has been served on you so that you can use it, if you wish, in cross-examination, of Mr. Stijovic. Now we will hear from the witness. If the witness would take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. If you'd like to take a seat. Examined by Mr. Nice:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is, I think, Sir Peter de la Billiere, and, Sir Peter, you are a retired general of the British army, retiring at the top-rank level in that army?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to turn to items of your curriculum vitae in a minute, but in order to make them --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In order to make the items of your curriculum vitae of particular relevance, it may help if we look first at the task to which you have responded by the report you have prepared. General, were you asked to look at and consider various documents concerning the Yugoslav army?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: I was. A wide range of documents concerning the background, doctrine, and structure of the Yugoslav army were made available to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You looked at them in no way as an expert on that particular army; would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: That is correct. I had not had personal experience with the Yugoslav army, nor have I ever visited the country.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so your expertise, as a soldier, is about armies in general, and then looking at what the documents show, and only what the documents show, of this army in particular; correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in that way, you bring -- it's for the Judges to decide in due course to what extent, but you bring detached rather than involved knowledge to bear?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: That is correct. I bring knowledge of having served for 41 years, much of it overseas, frequently with foreign armies, right through the ranks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And before we turn to your curriculum vitae, one last question: Although, of course, all armies are unique unto themselves, do they in fact, in your experience, have common characteristics, common behaviour patterns, and so on, that enable an experienced soldier such as yourself to look at the construction of another army and to form opinions about how things will have happened?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: There is bound to be great similarity of doctrine and command in any well-structured, well-managed, well-trained army, whether it be my own army or foreign armies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then finally, to establish the ground rules under which you operated for this project: So far as facts are concerned, did you work on the basis that the facts -- that's the underlying facts, not the facts relating particularly to the accused, but the underlying facts that were, as alleged in the indictment, recognising, of course, that it's a matter for later whether those facts are established and made out?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: That is absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if we turn to the end of your report - and I trust that you have a copy of your report with you - and the biographical information begins at -- or is annex A and comes after page 29, you've set out your whole career there, but perhaps the most material parts for this -- for the purposes of this report includes, as you've already said, that you served overseas for a large part of your career; correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: That is correct; east --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Korea, in Egypt and elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: Correct, and widely in the Middle East and the Far East.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You spent some, is it, 20 in the special air services at, I think, all or most commissioned-rank positions?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: I served in the special air service on and off, because one is never a permanent member of that organisation, one is always attached from elsewhere. On and off I served for a total of 20 years, from the rank of lieutenant to the most senior rank within the organisation, which was brigadier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that work, did those postings, bring you into contact with insurgent battles of one kind or another?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: Ostensibly, throughout the Middle East and the Far East, and of course, on counter-insurgency matters within the United Kingdom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To that extent, it may be of particular relevance when looking at the response of the Yugoslav army to what may be described, depending on terminological choice, as terrorism, insurgency, freedom fighting, whatever it may be?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: That would be so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in the course of those postings, did you have contact with and get to have experience with a range of foreign armies?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: I did. I did two full secondments to foreign armies, serving under the command of those foreign armies as opposed to under the direct command of the British army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then over the page: Did you at a later date, perhaps within the overall period of your working with the SAS, become involved and responsible for establishing the British military counter-terrorist force, working in conjunction with British police against mainland terrorist threats in the United Kingdom?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this an example of several or many where you had to cooperate with and deal with police forces?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: I have worked extensively on police military operations, both in my own army and in my own country, and particularly overseas, on operations in the Far East and to some extent also in the Middle East.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before moving on from that general type of operation, it's important to bear in mind, it may be, that some countries have third forces, I think you might describe it, that's a militarised police force, and some, like the United Kingdom, do not. Have you ever yourself had to work with a police force that contains this third force?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: I have, in Malaysia, and of course I have some experience of it where I've worked in cooperation with overseas armies and where we have had to work with the police, but that has been somewhat limited experience in that particular instance. In Malaysia, though, I had a wide experience of working with the police on combat operation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Shortly after the conclusion of the Falklands war, you served in the Falklands as the military commissioner and military commander, I think.

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: I had overall command exercised from the United Kingdom of the SAS operations in the Falklands, and then subsequently I was appointed, after I had attended the Royal College of Defence studies, the most senior Defence college in the United Kingdom, I was appointed the military commissioner and commander of British forces in the Falkland Islands, where I served for 14 months.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, there, but I think also elsewhere, did you have close experience of working not just with soldiers but also with local politicians?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: I was a member of the legislative council, which was the governing body of the Falkland Islands, and as such, had responsibilities to the civil commissioner, who was more or less of equal rank to myself, and for the management of the country, or the islands, and the restructuring of the islands. I was also commander of the British forces there, and that included all three services: Navy, army, and air force.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The interaction of military and political commands is something you deal with in your report, but is it something that occurs at various levels of seniority in armies and something with which you have direct experience yourself?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Could you repeat that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Interaction of military and political authorities is something that I think you will say happens at various levels of command in the army, various senior levels of command; and is that something with which you, one way and another, have direct experience?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: I have had extensive experience in that field, most of it at more senior rank level, and indeed, diplomacy in a senior commander in an army is a major aspect of his work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Penultimately, dealing with things broadly chronologically, did you -- were you appointed to command the British forces in the Gulf War?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thus being in command of how many men and women?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: Up to a total of about 44, 45.000, from all three services in the merchant fleet, and indeed any British resources that were in theatre. Of course, I had a senior commander within the United Kingdom to whom I reported and I also dealt directly with British ministers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in that operation, did you have contact not only with the American but with other armies as well?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: Widely, particularly the Americans, obviously, who provided the commander-in-chief in the field, but also with a wide range of Arab armies and other European armies, notably the French.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if we deal with matters broadly chronologically, there's one I think that may be out of broad chronological sequence, and that is the well-known Iranian siege in London. Your role in that?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: I was the brigadier commanding the special air service at the time, and my role there was to have a permanent seat in the government briefing room, cabinet office briefing room, where I was able to advise on the role and possible opportunities for military forces, SAS forces in this case, should they have been required by the police. It was a police operation with the police in overall command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this was an operation with police, military, and of course, political involvement?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: Very much so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, now, with all that experience and your knowledge of -- and experience of foreign armies, you looked at the documentation relating to this army, and if we can indeed detach ourselves from the particular terminology of the report, which is summarised both in an overview and in concluding paragraphs, before we just look at a couple of exhibits and a couple of passages in the report itself, which otherwise becomes admitted as evidence: How are you able to -- what conclusions did you make about this army's performance in the Kosovo period on the basis of the various assumptions we set out at the beginning of your evidence?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: Well, you must understand this is all done from briefing and from notes, not from personal experience on the ground. Therefore, I have looked at the structure of the Yugoslav army, as I understand it was at the time, and the doctrine, that is to say, the way in which the army practiced and effectively ran its military operations. And I was greatly impressed with the detail into which they went. I was greatly impressed with the attention to the care and understanding of humanitarian issues that was included in them. I looked at the laws for the Yugoslav army and found them to be highly commendable, and indeed, to be honest, when I finished reading all of this, I thought that it would be very appropriate if it was provided in the British army, as indeed it is very similarly. So it's a thoroughly well-structured format for an army of high quality people. I then looked at the charges raised in the indictment, which is all I have to go on in terms of what actually happened on the ground and how these rules were applied, and I have to say that I found them totally out of line and not in any way reflecting the very commendable structure and doctrine of the Yugoslav army. They were widespread on the ground, frequently with several incidents, major incidents, taking place at one time, and in my opinion, anybody who was involved in those operations was not following the law of the Yugoslav army, nor the doctrine of the Yugoslav army as it has been presented to me. And I believe that the activities were so widespread, involving such large numbers of the civilian community, that the force levels necessary in the field to implement what went on were such that they must have been controlled and commanded under the military system. Also, if I bear in mind the media presentation, together with the formal normal and expected reporting system that operated within the Yugoslav army, in no way could these have been conducted without the knowledge, and presumably support and maybe even direction, of the most senior ranks in that army and thereby, by implication, the political overall command of that army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I was proposing to do was to touch on a just few points of the report and to look in detail at one or two of the exhibits, and that will be all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The little bundle that you have with tab numbers, somewhat inconveniently doesn't have tab numbers matching footnote exhibit references. I'm sorry about that, but in the best-organised offices, sometimes things don't go quite perfectly. General, if you would be good enough, please, to take your report, and you've already touched on this once, but given that the learned Judges may have no or no immediate military experience of their own to go on, and there are others who have none of any kind, can you just help us with what is clearly a term of art, a doctrine, an army's doctrine. It features first on page 1, three lines up from the bottom. Is a doctrine something that, when spoken of by people such as yourself exist in a single document or is it something that is to be identified as coming from the overall documentation regulating an army?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: Any properly managed army develops a doctrine which is, in effect, in civilian parlance, I suppose, is the theory, the overall concept in which that army will conduct its operations and the framework within which the army can be expected to develop its operational planning and orders, and it is therefore an important set of guidelines which one would expect to be from time to time updated as the operational threat changed or adjusted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: What I've tried to do is to, in my first seven pages, is to illustrate examples of the doctrine as portrayed by the Yugoslav army from the documents that were put in front of me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And in that regard, because the pages substantially speak for themselves, I'm going to ask you, please, to look only at one exhibit in detail, I think, and that is the footnote 4 on page 3, which is tab 2 in the little bundle, and is the battle order, or the attack order - I beg your pardon - that you refer to and suggest is a good example of the applied VJ doctrine.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Chamber has that document, which is, I have to say, one of the very limited number of orders available to the OTP. Perhaps I can just pause there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any observation to make, General, about the quantity of documentary material available for inspection?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: Well, to be honest, I was extremely surprised at the lack of it, particularly bearing in mind that we're talking of a properly structured, properly trained and educated army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What would you expect by way of retained, and thus available, orders in such an army?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: Sorry. Say that again, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What would you expect, in terms of quantity, by way of retained orders that should be available to a body like this Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: A wide range of conventional papers, such as the daily sitrep reports, the operational orders issued, right from the top, right the way down through the chain of command, to certainly brigade and possibly battalion level. The war diary is -- a war diary is a diary that is kept by the operational staff at various levels of command, itemising what has taken place during any one day, and indeed in specific times, and there is normally a specific staff officer who would be allocated to keeping that sort of document. And really, a complete lack of documentation at all, implying that the operations must, to a very large extent, have -- assuming these documents don't exist at all, they must have been conducted, to a very large extent, on verbal orders, with no proper records being kept.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Alternatively, that such records haven't been found?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if we look at this document dated the 13th of February, 1999, I think one of the first things that is obvious to you, with your experience, is that there are some things missing from it.

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: Well, the first thing is, of course, it -- on page 1, Your Honour, top left-hand corner, it says "strictly confidential number." There's no number there, and I would have -- certainly a classified military document would normally have a number that would enable it to be kept very closely under control so it didn't get lost and perhaps abused, and if it did, one would identify which document had been lost. The other notable omission is right at the end, Your Honour, where, of course, it would appear that it's unsigned, and the conclusion I draw from that is that maybe it was a draft or maybe it has been introduced for some other reason. It's not for me to speculate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But taking it, then, at its face value, having made those -- it also doesn't have a distribution list, does it, I think?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: No distribution. Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Taking it at its face value, with its headings "Enemy," then - this is on page 1 of the document - "Neighbours," "I have decided," "Tasks," and so on, with one or two exceptions, how does this compare to the sort of order you would find in either the British army or any other similarly well-organised, well-structured, well-communicating army?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: It follows a recognisable pattern. The actual headings used vary from what I'm used to in my own army, obviously, and that's not surprising, but actually, their meaning is identical. And if I can give you an example. Well, if we just take the first page, the enemy is the enemy. That stays the same with us too. "Neighbours," we would call them friendly forces. And then "I have decided," which the Yugoslav army seemed to put a great deal of effort and concentration into getting the decision process working, and rightly so too, we would call it the aim, or the mission. I won't go on with the rest of the document, but you can see the pattern is that it's a formal layout that is instantly recognisable by anybody who has had military experience.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This particular order -- General, I may be making a mistake that I really shouldn't be making, namely, coming in too soon after your answer with my question. Even though we're in the same language, we should leave a gap because of the translation. On page 2, paragraph 5, line 4, I see a reference to the Kosovska Mitrovica PJP company, which is a special group. And then over on page 3, right at the top, we can see: "In implementing the tasks, ensure full cooperation with MUP organs in the general zone of combat operations." We see a reference at the foot of 6.2 to combat operations conducting reconnaissance by engaging reconnaissance forces. At the last paragraph before 6.3, we see a further reference to the MUP, in this quotation: "During the attack, focus security on protecting tanks and other combat ordnance from close-range DTS actions, particularly in wooded or intersected terrain, and also engage MUP forces in this." So what does this order tell you about the involvement of other forces, which we can also see reflected on page 5, at 7.5, with the fourth- line reference to prisoners of war to be handed over after interrogation to the MUP? What does this tell you about the integration of forces?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: It is quite clearly that in these operations the police and the military were occupying very much the same geographical territory, and, very sensibly, they have coordinated their operations to work in harmony and to use each other's resources to best effect for the operations that they had in hand. And this operation order clearly tells the military members of the forces in the region how they should collaborate with the police. And if I may say so, they are sensible instructions, instructions that you would expect to see when you had a police field force and a military field force operating together in a combat area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I ask one more question on this document before, if the Chamber so decides, the time has come for a break? On page 4, in the second and third unnumbered subparagraphs, summarised: 1) Withdraw civilians, for reasons of their safety and to avoid their being used as shields; and the second subparagraph -- and I should really have made arrangements to lay this on the overhead projector. I'm sorry about that. I didn't do that. Too late, I think. Second subparagraph - thank you - to forbid looting of property. Those would be things you would approve, I suspect, as appropriate to find in the orders of a properly performing army.

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: If the army was operating in a counter-terrorist situation, from their perspective, I would expect them to have clear directions as to how they were to handle the civilian population, and one of the problems they would have would indeed be the need to separate the terrorists, who may be shielding behind the civilian community, from that civilian community, and the army would have a responsibility for that. I cannot say that they would always get it right if the terrorists are clever enough to conduct themselves in such a way that they incorporate the civilian population. But generally speaking, what they have outlined there is a sensible, humanitarian, military understanding of the difference between the civilian community and the terrorist community who may come from that very civilian community, and that is perhaps an example of the military doctrine which we were talking about earlier on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's clearly a convenient time for a break. Sir Peter, we're going to adjourn now for 20 minutes. I must give you the warning which I give to all witnesses: Please not to speak to anybody about your evidence until it's over, and that does include the Prosecution team. We'll adjourn now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the document we were considering and that I omitted to put on the overhead projector has already been produced by General Drewienkiewicz as tab 47 in Exhibit 94. I don't know that it needs to be reproduced by this witness. Before I move on to ask other questions, the Chamber will have observed that several of his footnotes relate to the VJ manual of 1997 on command and control, and in the tabs we have - and I'm not going to take us to all of them, they're there for convenience - these are -- this manual is reproduced in part, very limited part, in tabs 1, 3, 4, 5, 6, and 7. Sorry: 1, 3, 4, 5, and 7. And it's suggested that it might be prudent now to give that manual, which I know is already before the Chamber, an exhibit number. The document itself is, of course, a full binder, which I hold up. And if that's a convenient way of dealing with it, because the general has already relied on it in his conclusions and in his report, may it be exhibited?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. It can have a new number.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think it's been made available to everyone already, and therefore we don't need to distribute multiple copies.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be marked Prosecutor's Exhibit 309.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, in looking at that particular exhibit, and the other materials you set out in page 1 to 7, your conclusion, as already advanced on more than one occasion, is that in writing, or on paper, a well-organised army of the type you would easily enough recognise?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The question of how its appearance on paper contrasts with or fits with the facts that you have taken from the indictment is a matter you've really already commented on, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: Yes, I have, and it doesn't dovetail.
