utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to look at the structure of your report, we go, then, from page 7, headed "Command in Practice," and we can deal with the next few pages again, I think quite briefly. But on page 7 itself, you make reference, at the foot of the page, in the paragraph beginning with there, that in an internal security situation such as existed in the FRY - and you accept that whether they're insurgents, terrorists or whatever else, they present an internal security situation for these purposes - your experience is that the police would expect to be represented at a high level of operational command and to play an influential role?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: Your Honour, you could not have two separate forces operating in the field without them being properly coordinated and working to a joint plan, certainly not in a well-structured and well-managed army such as the Yugoslav army purported to be, and because, apart from everything else, it would lead to fratricide it would lead to disharmony and lack of coordination of operations, and indeed, you wouldn't be making sensible use of the forces that were available to you unless you combined their operations under an overall mission.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the same topic, one other point, and it's on the following page, page 8, and it's the last three lines, or three and a bit lines, of that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before I ask you to deal with it, Your Honour, I think that expert reports are produced, are they not, as exhibits in the case? And it may be, again, as a courtesy to those following, to lay the relevant extracts on the overhead projector, if that accords with the Chamber's accepted practice. Before it's done, is -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Produce the report and give it an exhibit number, that would be a sensible thing to do. If the usher would be good enough to, with the overhead projector in operation --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, this will be marked Prosecutor's Exhibit 310.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If the usher could stand by the overhead projector, with a copy of the report, which is coming your way, and just ensure that the relevant pages are capable of being viewed. We're now on, if you look at the bottom, page 8 of 29, the top paragraph of that. Sorry not to have organised this before. Entirely my oversight. Page 8 of 29. Thank you very much. Just lay that, the top part of that on the overhead projector. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You make this point in your report, General: That it's worth mentioning that if the police were placed under military command, you put it in this way: They would expect to have a right of appeal direct to the civil authorities and to the police leadership if they considered they were misemployed or given illegal orders. And the question I would ask you: How can you be so sure of that? How can you express that view with confidence?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: When a force is put under some form of control of another force, whether it be an army under the command or control of a foreign army or whether it be a force like the police force or under command of -- working with the army, you -- its own chain of command would still remain extant. And if we take this particular instance, if you were a policeman working in cooperation with the army, then you would not abdicate and close down your right to use your own police chain of command and have access to it should you feel the need, for whatever reason. And it may also, of course, be for logistic reasons as well as for concerns about the way the operations were being conducted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we turn over to page 9, at the foot of that page, you've moved on to deal with joint and combined arms operations. Just in a sentence, please, first of all, distinguish between joint and command -- joint and combined, please.

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: Well, this is my definition, and obviously based on my personal experience. A joint operation would be similar, for example, to that which took place in the Gulf, where you had a variety of armies and organisations working together under a joint command. A combined operation would be more an organisation combining the resources of its own structure. For example, in the case of the military, perhaps the artillery, the engineers, the infantry, and you would combine -- that would be a combined operation. But these are terminology and I'm sure they may vary from different interpretations in foreign armies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Well, then, let's turn over to the next page and look at one more exhibit in a little detail. Page 10 has, towards the foot, a quotation set out, and it's footnote 8, but it's -- in the Chamber's and accused's and amici's bundle, it is tab 6 in full, and it's a public announcement of the Yugoslav army's chief of staff, then General Pavkovic. And the extract - thank you very much - the extract you quote, which we can see on the overhead projector, reads as follows, and it's at the foot of the page in tab 6. It reads: "It is true that the national Defence Law regulated that the police units in the responsibility zones were bound to subordinate to the commands of the Yugoslav army. However, this never came into existence, and one should not wave with police force records on their submission which had not been duly applied. The police had their own headquarters, headed by their own officers, and the cooperation with the army was coordinated through political actors in joint command, formed for the purpose. Therefore, the information to what the police force units were doing can best be provided by police commanders and the members of the joint command in charge of them." Now, your comment on that, please. I mean, you've set it out in your report, but again if you can put this in your own words.

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, I'd like to just expand a bit on this relationship between the police and the military, because I think in this particular situation and similar ones, it is the greatest importance. First of all, you cannot have, as I've already stated, the police, or any other organisation, running one operation and the military running another. There has got to be coordination if there's not going to be chaos and fratricide. The next question is where does that coordination come in? It must come in at all levels. For example, if you have a company operation - and I hope I may assume that people understand the level of command I'm talking about - then if that is going to have police support, as indeed that operation that we looked at earlier implied, there must be an understanding and communication between the police and the army at that level. Now, that communication may be filled by the provision of a liaison officer in the army headquarters, or vice versa, it may be filled or assisted by the provision of radio communications between the two, because it is unlikely that the police radio and the military radio are compatible, but it would have to be there, otherwise there would be no cooperation in the operations. And therefore, the follow-up from that is that both the police and the army must know what each other are doing, because they're in mutual support. Now, you can extend that right the way up the chain of command, because for the police to be placed under any form of control by the army, or ordered to take -- to conduct an operation in concert with the army, the orders for that to the police must come down the police network, and that implies that at the top of that network, such cooperation and coordination has been agreed. So although we may be, in one instance, talking about a company operation, a relatively small operation, the policy behind that cooperation would have come down from the most senior levels in the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: General, when you say that the police must know what the army is doing, that would be in an ideal situation, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would be necessary, Your Honour, if you were to avoid a conflict of activity which could lead to fratricide between the two -- that means to say the army shooting the police accidently because they didn't know what the police were doing, or vice versa. So I would say it is an essential situation if the two were going to cooperate together on operations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, the quotation from General Pavkovic, can you just remind: What context was that given?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is a public announcement that he made. I'm afraid I was looking myself just now for the date, but I think it's sometime after June 13th, 2001, because it's responsive by him to a press conference statement by the Serbian police minister at the time, Dusan Mihajlovic. And it deals with a number of matters, but it deals here in the paragraph with his position as having been in charge of the 3rd army. He's saying he's not ashamed of a single decision, records of witnesses, everyone knows what he was doing during the aggression, and those who were calling him to account were the ones whose whereabouts were unknown at the time when it was most difficult and dangerous. And then he goes on, repeating that the national defence law regulated the police units in responsibility zones, but going on to make the point that he does in the extract we've -- or rather, the witness has quoted. So that it's a response by the then general to Dusan Mihajlovic's press conference statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you make the point, I think, General, that it's difficult to understand, and in your judgement is implausible, that there should be any implication that the one did not know what the other was doing through the joint command.

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: If they were running operations, military operations and one in support of the other, whether it was military support in the form of artillery in support of the police, or whether it was police support as implied in that earlier exhibit I produced, an operation order helping the army guarding its tanks or looking after prisoners, there must be cooperation and there must be coordination at all levels, yes. And indeed, I think it is implied in the area because, if I remember correctly, Kosovo was commanded by a committee that incorporated the police as well as the military and civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, may the -- thank you. May the public announcement of Lieutenant General Pavkovic be produced as an exhibit? I think it's in a binder. I'm not sure that it is in the binder. May it just be produced?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, how do you propose to produce these exhibits? Do you want this one done separately?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think this one done separately. That's the only one I'm going to produce, apart from the manual we've already produced, through this witness. Everything else comes in through Mr. Coo or is already in under others such as General Drewienkiewicz.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be marked Prosecutor's Exhibit 311.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm quite happy, if it's convenient to the Chamber, of course, to produce the tabbed file as a separate exhibit. That will, of course, be duplicative of other materials. I'm in the Chamber's hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think that will simply lead to confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, if we then look -- and I needn't ask for this to go on the ELMO, because we can go over it very quickly. Starting at page 11, you deal with various aspects of coordination, some of which you've touched on and others of which I'm happy to leave with the Chamber in written form. "Diplomatic" you've touched on, "Flanking Units" you've touched on, "Air" may be read by those wishing to, and "Special Operations" you deal with on page 13, "Fire Support" follows and then "Police" on page 14. And if we go over to page 15 of the report, please, Usher, and lay that on the overhead projector. A couple of amplifications on that. At the top of the page -- well, the first new paragraph, beginning "In all these various operational relationships..." you express a view in relation to a well-organised army, such as this appears to be, that: "it is important to remember that if military and police units are working in harmony, whatever the command relationship, there will normally be an exchange of --" you then say -- "twice daily situation reports," sitreps. Just pausing there, you volunteered "twice." Can you explain that or comment on it.

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: Yes. Nobody can command a complex operation from a more senior perspective, shall we say, of brigadier level unless he knows what is going on, and so he's got to have a regular flow of information in the form of reports and the formal side, the routine side, we call sitreps, situation reports. But they will come through more frequently, depending upon the intensity of the operations. And if he doesn't get those, then he's not in command. And furthermore, if he's going to be in command, he must know and understand what the ground is like that his forces are operating under, so he would be expected to supplement these with visits into the field. Depending upon his style, I would suggest any sensible commander up to brigadier level would be visiting units in the field, and possibly at a higher-rank level, visiting units in the field at least once a day. The situation reports really are the life blood of command, and without them, the system would perish.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That obviously, from what you say, it applies to the British army. Is there any reason to believe it's any different in any other well-organised army?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: You cannot run military operations, or indeed business operations, for that matter, without having the information on which senior commanders will have to make decisions and decide such things as to whether reinforcements are to be brought in, redeployments are to be made, and the multitude of day-to-day issues that have to be decided on up the chain of command in any military operation. It is -- I can only repeat that it is essential that information is passed to them to enable these decisions to be taken on the facts and not on what I call armchair generalship.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And if the information, General, was not passed in that way, what conclusion are you drawing from that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If no information was passed up the chain of command and the people in the command chain were not commanding the troops under their -- or the police under their control, they had abrogated their responsibility, or those units that were carrying out operations on their own and independently were operating illegally, really, outside the instructions they had been given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You then express the view that we can see on the screen: You don't believe such vast movements of people and killings as alleged in the indictment could take place without the local VJ army commander being fully aware, and in reaching that conclusion, you've taken into account your understanding on occasions that the VJ provided direct fire and other support for police actions?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. There's one thing I want to ask you about, Rules of Engagement, which is the following section, but it's really on the following page. By and large, I don't wish to amplify what's in your report, but you describe how, at subparagraph B on page 16, as an example of Rules of Engagement at the lowest -- not the lowest level, but the most junior level, individual soldiers may be told they can only open fire in self-defence, and then after they've been challenged, threatening force three times. This is just an example. But you then say, "Each soldier might be given detailed instructions to this effect in written form." Is that practice, written instructions to the individual soldiers, widespread in well-organised armies or not, or can't you say?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: I don't think I can say that. I put that in as an example of the sort of attention to detail that would be necessary if soldiers on the ground are going to be fully comprehensive of the level of force that the civilian authorities and the military authorities are delegating to them. There are other ways of doing it, I'm sure. That is the most effective way, in my experience, because the man's got it written in front of him and he can look at it from time to time. But if you didn't do that, if you issue it as orders, then those orders must be issued, otherwise a soldier doesn't know when he can open fire. Perhaps I could add that in a full-scale war, such as we'll say the Gulf war or even Falkland Islands operations, in my experience, you reach a point where the politicians delegate effectively a free-fire authority to the military commander and that enables him to use all the forces at his disposal to the fullest effect. But in insurgency operations, such as I suspect is implied in this case, it is very much more complex and the politicians will want to keep a very tight control over how the army, and indeed the police, behave so that they do not disrupt whatever the political policy may be for that region. And that is when you have got to have the clearest of clear instructions, all the way down the chain of command, as to what level of force you can use and when and how you can use it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The section on Discipline starts at page 17. Some of these you have covered already and the rest I'm going to leave for the report itself. But you may be able to help us with a couple of points. On page 22 - we can put that on the overhead projector, please - you already having dealt with the need for discipline and in particular the need for swift and peremptory disciplinary decisions in battle or war, but on page 22, in the first complete paragraph - absolutely right - beginning, "In any war ..." Thank you, Usher. You speak of the likelihood of individual incidents involving excessive or criminal violence and the mishandling of the situation at the junior levels and possibly even up to that of company command. You say such incidents would normally be identified, disciplinary action taken, although in the heat of battle this can take time and evidence prove not to be readily forthcoming. You then make this observation: "The excesses as described in the indictment would, however, require a massive logistic and manpower organisation in the first place, to initiate them by driving people unwillingly from their homes, and secondly, to carry them out with the efficiency and expedition that was their clear hallmark." Anything you want to add to that, and just to make sure we understand what the hallmark is you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: The hallmark I'm referring to comes back really to this control of the forces and passage of information and the force levels you're allowed to use. All these things come together. Now, when I look at the indictment and see the numbers of civilians that were moved -- and I have to assume, Your Honour, that this is what happened. Whether it did or whether it's been proven or not, I have no idea, but this is what I'm basing my comments on. When I see the extent of what I can only describe as a concerted assault on a civilian community and the numbers involved, and the numbers of people that it is suggested have been killed en bloc as opposed to in military operations where, by definition, people not be killed in great numbers in one place because they're looking after themselves and military men are protecting their lives, then one can only say that it must have been an operation that was authorised and directed. This was no rogue operation by a break-away company or even a break-away brigade. This was a concerted policy, political policy, being interpreted and acted upon by the military and the police, I assume, in this area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps at page 24, one point for emphasis, in relation to discipline amongst other topics, and it's at the first fresh paragraph on page 24. You postulate here for such armies as we are concerned with that: "In general terms, in a military hierarchy, units and formations will be aware in some detail of the actions required of their troops at least two steps down the hierarchy." And you then give us an example that a commander of a brigade would expect to have an understanding of the activities of the company. Is that a matter that has been reflected in your experience of Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 9582 to 9594. armies around the world?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: Yes. Obviously it's pursued with mixed diligence by different commanders, but it's a very indicative rule of thumb that, to give you a feel for how far down a chain of command a senior commander should be thinking and taking detailed responsibility for without actually interfering in the minutiae of operations which, if the orders are clear and the directions are clear, will be being conducted by the more junior people in the chain of command, according to their task in support of the overall strategy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Page 25 brings us to your consideration of the possibility of rogue units, and within that you break down misjudgement into three possibly useful categories for consideration. I beg your pardon. You break down rogue units by reference to three categories, the first of which is misjudgement, the second of which is overreaction, and the third of which is deliberate divergence. And then on page 26, the foot of page 26, having dealt above, and we needn't look at it, with the need for superiors to institute disciplinary proceedings, your conclusion in relation to the possibility of mere overreaction is to be found at the foot of the page: "I cannot support any claim which states that the events in Kosovo, as described in the indictment and other documents I have reviewed, were the products of misjudgements by junior commanders. The wide scale and the media coverage of the excesses undermine any such claim as does the failure to take adequate disciplinary measures." And then you raise as a possibility there must have been collusion, at best, "at senior command level and, at worst, the senior military command knew that subordinate commanders were operating under directions to follow such a policy and turned a blind eye." Is that your opinion?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: Without any ambiguity at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Anything you need to add to that or does it stand --

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: I think it -- really, the points I've already made on responsibility for operation, command and control and the passage of information and the coordination of the forces involved illustrates how impossible it would be for units -- for such a large area and such an enormous operation as moving these numbers of people and killing these numbers of people as is purported to have taken place in the indictment could happen unless it was properly directed and coordinated. I mean, to move people, even if you don't look after them and don't do anything for them, requires transport and logistics and passage through country without them being interfered with and issues like that, which in themselves require coordination by the military or by whoever is carrying out those operations. So these operations were, without doubt, directed and coordinated and not the odd commander going berserk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your third category under this heading, is deliberate divergence, which we see on page 27, and you see with the possibility of deliberate divergence and indeed probably some historically well-known examples one could refer to if necessary. You make the point, on page 27, that this could only happen for a short period of time in a well-regulated army. And then in the middle of the page, you make this point about the law on the army of Yugoslavia - it's conveniently on the screen - saying it is "a commendable and tightly-worded document to which any nation could be proud." You stick to that view, do you?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: Without any ambiguity, it is a fine document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The conclusion of that, beside the facts as you take them to be from the indictment, is, of course, the conclusion that follows four lines afterwards, namely, that the thrust of the operations in Kosovo must have conformed to the wishes of the military chain of command.

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And we can, I think, move straight away to your conclusions on page 29, where, at the top of the page, you're dealing with the police, and you've already, I think, covered this last paragraph in part, where you were dealing with the free fire possibility for non-insurgency conflicts. And here a different topic and differently expressed, you say that from what you've read, it's not possible to identify -- sorry -- that you don't think that the possibility existed, based on the description you've read, whereby it was not possible to identify or report excesses because of the high intensity of operations. They weren't engaged, Serb forces weren't engaged in a constant, high-intensity battle against a large, conventional army and would have had time properly to assess information being reported by units in the field and other sources such as the media. In your opinion, no recourse to the "fog of war" argument.

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: Absolutely, and so the information was there at the time. I should emphasise that even in a major military or full-scale operation, I would be a very unhappy commander if I didn't know what was going on. But what I'm saying is that the detail of what was going on might not be given the attention that it would be in a counter-insurgency operation. In a counter-insurgency operation, the detail of what is going on is of the utmost importance right the way up the chain of command if the government policy is to be implemented at the front-line level, and I would suggest that the detail of the operations in this case, whatever they were, were available up the chain of command, must have been.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And thus, your conclusion, which you've already forecast and dealt with, in the word Summary and in what follows?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: I have no cause to adjust that or change it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just leave that on the overhead projector for those who wish to read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And Your Honour, I'm reminded helpfully by Ms. Graham, that there is perhaps one other of the items referred to in the folder exhibited, or extract of exhibits, that should be produced. It is tab 9, I think, which is footnote 11, which Your Honours can find -- I've passed over and I don't intend to return to it. It can be found on page 17 and is in the Rules of Engagement section. The document concerned is a booklet. The description is on -- it's Application of the Rules of International Law of Armed Conflict. It's a book that covers how the Yugoslav army respected the laws of armed conflict, with examples being given. It's a straightforward printed book of this kind, and may we produce photocopies of the book and the book itself as a specific exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the usher return.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be marked Prosecutor's Exhibit 312.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Those are the only questions I ask the general. Thank you very much. If you'd wait there, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic, it's for you to cross-examine.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May I know in advance whether you're going to restrict my time at all?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. An hour and a half we'll give you. Up to an hour and a half, of course.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think, Mr. May, that that is too little time, in view of the extensive material contained in the general's report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us see how you get on and what progress you make.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, I have to say that things are made easier by the fact that the general has provided logical answers, and without doubt, when it comes to the documents in question, he interpreted them as they in fact read. But of course there are other problems which are put in two different ways, and they are two-fold, with respect to the differences that there are in views, the views presented by the other side, the opposite side, and what it is suggesting. But let me go on to the questions. Cross-examined by Mr. Milosevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, according to what the Prosecution has asserted - I don't think that it can be contested - that you are a military expert, are you not?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: I don't like the word of "expert." I have had a wider experience than many people in certain military areas, and I've had some just short of 41 years in military service, so I certainly know a certain amount about military affairs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, without a doubt, and I'm not questioning that at all from the aspects of your very rich career but from the aspects of the way in which this fact is being used and utilised by the opposite side. Because I have -- I'm in a relationship with the opposite side here and not with you, General, so they have denoted you as a military expert, and that is not contested in the paper drawn up by Mr. Dirk Ryneveld. That's what it says. And did you entitle your report "Report of the Prosecution Military Expert," or was that the title provided by the Prosecution? Did you yourself write down that title of your report, or was it the Prosecution? At the top, the header, what we have received, it says, "Report of the Prosecution Military Expert, General Sir Peter de la Billiere." Are those your words, your heading, or was that one provided by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: It was a phrase that was well used during our dialogue when I put this report together. I did not write those words personally. I did, however, support them and acknowledge them when I signed my name to the statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. However, in the last paragraph of your c.v., your biography, you say you don't see yourself as an expert in affairs of the Yugoslav army or the conflict in Kosovo. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: That is absolutely correct, and my information on those affairs has been presented to the Court, the basis of my information on those affairs, and thus my comment is not based on personal experience of the Yugoslav army; it is based on the documentary evidence that has been put in front of me and before the Court as to how the Yugoslav army operated or was purported to have operated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. So I can take that to mean a certain relativisation on your part of the degree of competence when it comes to the Yugoslav army and the Kosovo -- conflict in Kosovo, and not in any regard to your general knowledge of military skills, military profession, or military experience?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, do you consider that you are quite clear on the conflicts and the causes of the conflicts - and I should like to underline the word "causes"- the causes of the conflicts in Kosovo during 1998, as well as the nature of the conflict itself during that same period of time?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: My knowledge is from two sources. I had a general knowledge of what went on and a general interest in what went on, obviously, from a professional point of view and from a national point of view. But I would not wish to say that that knowledge is sufficient for me to make a judgement, personal judgement, on how the Yugoslav army behaved. I then have another level of knowledge, which is that provided by the documents put in front of me, and those tell me, assuming that they were extant at the time, in great detail how the Yugoslav army and forces should have behaved and the structure of control and command that is purported to have existed out there. Now, I'm not in a position to say whether it did exist, but all I would say is that's what I was told I could assume and on that assumption that the documents put in front of me were reliable and extant, that is from what I drew my conclusions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in your considerations, did you dwell on the fact that Yugoslavia, starting out from the 24th of March, 1999, waged a defensive war against the greatest power that has existed in the world, which is to say NATO, the NATO pact, along with a simultaneous struggle against a very strong terrorist and strong terrorism working on part of its territory? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: I was fully aware of the general tenor of operations from the perspective of an educated, military educated person reading his newspapers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, in your military career, did you have any kind of experience whatsoever with the waging of a defensive war, that is to say, the kind of war in which you have to defend yourself when your country, mother country, is being attacked and which you are forced to wage on the ground and in the air in your own country's territory?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: Of course, going back to my young days, I was fully aware of what took place in the World War II, but I don't imagine that that is what you're really suggesting. I had probably more experience of defence, military defensive operations, than almost anybody left in the army by the time I retired, from the extremely intensive defence operations that I was involved in in Korea.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. On page 1 of your report, you say that the conclusions and opinions are based on your experience and your knowledge of your own, that is to say British, and other armed forces. "Opinions and conclusions in the report are based on my experience, including my knowledge of my own and other armed forces." That is what you state on page 1. Now, that is not in question, but my question is the following: When you compiled this report of yours, did you consult the facts? Did you look at the facts, specific facts linked to the problems that you are presenting your views on in the capacity of expert? And if so, could you please enumerate which sources you used and which facts you relied upon. Let me help you there. I have understood that the report was based and compiled on two parts of a military analyst of the Prosecution, Mr. Coo, and on the basis of various scanty documents, a few number of documents that you state, such as the manual of the army of Yugoslavia, leadership and command in 1997, command and control; Kosovo and Metohija, the application of international law in 1998 and 1999; the constitution of Yugoslavia; the law on national defence; and I see one order here by the commander, corps commander, Pristina Corps commander; and a statement put out from a press conference of some kind. Now, do you consider that these few elements that you have collected together would be sufficient for you to present a comprehensive view and have an overview of the comprehensive situation?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: I've made it quite clear where I have sourced my information concerning the structure and methods of operation of the Yugoslav army, and indeed you have helped me by reading many of them out. And I have --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's what I said, that I wish to help you.

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: Well, I have read the indictment, and that is the sole document on which I have made a judgement as to what happened on the ground, and it is not for me to comment on the accuracy or otherwise of the indictment. But from your perspective, and in order to assess how I came to the conclusions I came to, that is the information that I have used. I have not, for example, relied on my knowledge of press reports.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You just mentioned, General, if I can put it that way, a key element, one which brings into question the manner in which your knowledge was used, not when it comes to yourself personally, but how this was utilised by those people sitting opposite me over there. And I'm going to remind you, if I may -- I'm going to skip over one portion and go back to something else. Let me remind you of just a few quotations from this document of yours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I'm going to interrupt you again for length. You've been told often enough: You must ask questions which can be followed. Now, you can put to the witness a quotation and then ask him a question about it, but it's really very difficult to follow when you read out whole passages, as you tend to, and then expect witnesses to respond. Also, it's not for the witness, as you know, to listen to comments which you make about the Prosecution. You can make them to us, provided they're proper ones. Now, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I do have in mind the intellectual and educational level of the individual whom I'm questioning, so therefore I do not think that the general will not be able to understand what I'm asking him because the sentence is a longer one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But you're not to take up a long time by making speeches. Now, come on. What's the question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not making speeches, Mr. May. What I want to ask is something concerning what the general mentioned a moment ago. And I'm just going to quote two passages and then I'll go ahead with the question. They are quotations from his own reports, so he'll be able to recognise them. On page 15, at least it is 15 in my version. Of course, the English version is somewhat different, the pages in the English and B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But this is what you say, General: "Therefore, a military commander should be completely conscious of the workings of the police forces in his zone and also to be able to intervene and influence them," words to that effect. That is the introduction and the beginning of that sentence, but the essence is in the following: "I do not believe --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me find this, before we go on. It's apparently page 15 in the English. Do you have the passage, Sir Peter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, no, I haven't found it at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just let us find the passage. Now, Judge Kwon has it. Perhaps you'll refer the witness to it, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's the first fresh paragraph of page 15. It's in the middle part. "Thus the military commander would be fully aware of what the police forces would be doing." Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The point is in this following sentence: "I do not believe that such vast movements of people and killings as alleged in the indictment could take place without the local VJ commander being fully aware." As alleged in the indictment, therefore, could not take place without the full awareness of the local VJ commander. And then, several pages later, you go on to state the following --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. What is the question? You're referring to that passage, Mr. Milosevic. While we're dealing with it, what question do you have about it or what point do you want to make?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one more passage and then I have the same question that applies to both these passages and the entire approach, the whole approach of that so-called indictment. It is on page 21, and you're once again talking about the fact that in any war there is always the probability of there being individual incidents of overly great violence, et cetera. And then at the end of the paragraph, the sentence that I would like to read out is the following: "However, excessive behaviour described in the indictment require a massive logistic organisation, an organisation of manpower, in order to expel the people from their homes, firstly; and secondly, to carry them out with the efficiency and expedition that was their clear hallmark." So as you mentioned --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: General, have you that second passage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, what is the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, the substance of my question, and the entire approach here, is that the indictment for which they are using your knowledge in order to prove it, they are using your knowledge to prove the indictment, you are taking this to be proof of what is being claimed. Am I being clear enough? Is it, therefore, possible, because we have an indictment here before us, and I claim that the indictment is a false indictment, so we have an indictment which endeavours to prove itself and to take as evidence something that is being maintained. Now, if the indictment were clear and correct, the conclusion would be logical from the aspects of an expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you. This witness is not giving evidence about the indictment. He's made it quite plain. What he says is: Based on what is alleged in the indictment, these, as a military man, are my conclusions. Now, it's no good your arguing with him about the indictment. He's merely based his conclusions upon it and he's made it quite plain to us. So it is pointless talking about him coming to prove the indictment. He's doing no such thing. He's merely coming here to draw his conclusions from it. Now, have you any questions about those conclusions? See what he says. Now, if you've got any questions about that, ask them, but it's no good asking him about the indictment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I am not accusing the General, General de la Billiere, of having come here with any evil intentions. All I'm saying is that it is, on the part of this false indictment that we are abusing the fact that we have a military expert before us and that the indictment is taken to be proof in itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, it's not. I'm going to stop you. We've said this often enough before: The indictment is not proof in itself; it's merely what the Prosecution are setting out to prove. It's for us, as a Trial Chamber, to say whether it's true or not, and that we will do in due course, when we've heard the evidence. But there's no point trying to argue about it with this witness. Now, let's not waste any further time on that. If you've got questions about his conclusion or his report, of course you can ask it, but don't go on about the indictment any more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If I can clarify something. General, a minute ago I noticed you mentioned that the indictment was the sole document on which you have made a judgement as to what happened on the ground. Is it true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So what if later what is stated in the statement turns out to be not true in part or whole, then your observation is not true therefore, what is your observation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If the indictment is not -- well, I'm straying off my military territory here into legal territory, I fear, Your Honour, but if the indictment is not correct and not true, then clearly my conclusions would have to be either adjusted or, if it was not true at all, quite incorrect, they would be wrong. I have been asked to draw the conclusions that I drew based on the indictment. Now, it may well be that the details in the indictment will not be proven, and I think then people who have listened -- been kind enough to listen to my evidence will have to make a judgement as to whether those bits that are proven justify the conclusions I drew.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I shall proceed. However, this is the key issue, the key question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Of course it's the key question. It's the key question in the whole trial. Now, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, fine, now that we understand each other, that the indictment itself cannot be taken as proof of its very own truthfulness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, tell me, General: Do you think that the experience that you gained as a soldier in the campaigns of Great Britain in the Falklands or in the Gulf war can be applied in the case in Kosovo and Metohija in their entirety or partially or not at all?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: You draw out just two campaigns in my very diversified career, and certainly within those two campaigns there would be examples and lessons to be drawn and applied here. But I draw on a far wider experience, based in my involvement in full-scale military operations in Korea, through peace and military operations in Malaysia, through peace and military operations in Indonesia or on the borders of Indonesia, throughout military operations throughout the Middle East on many occasions, not just the Gulf War, and of course in my experience as - how can I put it without being immodest - my experience, considerable experience of dealing with counter-insurgents and counter-terrorist operations really over a period of decades.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You gained experience in wars in the so-called dependent territories, for example, in the Falklands, 13 and a half thousand kilometres away from the sovereign territory of Great Britain. And here you have a war that Yugoslavia waged on its very own sovereign territory, with its focus on very intensive terrorist activity taking place only 300 kilometres away from the capital of the country. So from the point of view of your own profession and your own personal convictions, do you give a sovereign state, as Yugoslavia is, the right to protect its sovereignty and territorial integrity on its very own territory? That is to say, do you think that this right is at least somewhat greater than the right of your own country to protect that right 13 and a half thousand kilometres away from its own sovereign territory?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: You draw on just one example --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't think this is a matter for the witness, really. It's probably a matter for us, if anybody.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. May. I assume that these are important questions, because let us go back to one that is linked to it. We spoke about the indictment a few minutes ago as the only document that the General took as a basis for drawing his own conclusions, and of course when the premises are wrong, even if the conclusions are right, they go in the wrong direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you also mentioned the media, General. Do you recall, for example, the press release of the state department at the beginning of April 1999 that half a million people were killed in Kosovo? Or the statement made by David Schaeffer [phoen], the American ambassador at large for war crimes, the one that he made on the 18th of April 1999, that hundreds of thousands of Albanians were killed in Kosovo, or spokesman Rubin, who said on the 19th of April, 1999, that hundreds of Albanians were killed? And also in May 1999, that 100.000 men were missing in Kosovo? So all these statements that were obviously launched as a pretext for the aggression against Yugoslavia, do they all become null and void before basic mathematics, that it goes down to a basic calculation? These hundreds of thousands are reduced to mere hundreds? Do you know how many persons were killed in this war in general and how many of them were found in Kosovo, how many dead persons were found in Kosovo? I'm just trying to explain this, because there is this political fog when speaking of repression.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We are going to stop you. Now, whether this has any relevance at all or not isn't clear, but we will ask the witness to answer the question. Sir Peter, do you know how many people were killed in Kosovo or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you please be so kind, Mr. May, as to tell the witness? Because it is very important for the way in which he can draw his conclusions. How many persons were found in Kosovo until now? How many dead bodies were found? So that I could put further questions to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... to him, but you can't convert the Presiding Judge into a witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, reference is made to the pre-war period, before the bombing, several hundreds, not several hundreds of thousands. And towards the end of the war, after the bombing, after the fighting between the KLA and the army and the police, all kinds of operations, the figure referred to is several thousand. So, General, is it clear that in political rhetoric about crimes, sometimes it is not clear in terms of defining this, but if we are talking about hundreds or hundreds of thousands, there is a distinction, a brilliant distinction, between the two. So justification for aggression against a country cannot be based on such mathematics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is way outside the evidence. Have you got a relevant question, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have many relevant questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. de la Billiere, do you think that motivation - and by saying that, I'm referring to the historical, ethnical, national, economical, military, et cetera factors - affect the course of an armed conflict, especially excessive incidents involved therein?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: I'm not clear as to what you mean by "motivation" in this context. You covered such a wide -- encompassed such a wide area for motivation, stretching from the economic to the business community, perhaps to military. Could we -- could I possibly ask you to be more precise, in a military sense, because that's what I'm here as, I'm here as a military witness, not an economic or political witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Let us say historic, emotional, ethnic, national, et cetera. So all of this that can comprise the motivation factor in a situation where one is defending one's homeland, in a situation when the enemy is all too cruel, when the enemy is committing all kinds of atrocities, torturing people, killing people, massacring them en masse. Do you think that that affects the intensity of the conflict, especially excessive incidents that may occur?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: I'm sure the motivational causes that you have outlined have an impact on the military forces - which is all the time competent in this court to talk about - on the military forces in the region of operations. And I would expect that the impact of these motivational issues to be taken into account when the overall employment of the military was decided upon at the highest command levels.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you notice in these scant documents -- and you yourself said that they were scant, although I do not see any reason why they should be scant, because the other party is duty-bound to make available to you all documents, not only some of them. Did you notice the concern of the entire chain of command to prevent any kind of excessive behaviour, to keep control, even to control fire, so that there would not be uncontrolled fire, to take care of prisoners of war, to take care of the civilian population, et cetera? Did you notice that in these documents?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: There was considerable -- a continuous thread in the limited documents that I saw concerning the operation - we've already discussed the lack of documents - of attention, notably in the book that my honourable compatriot produced here, to take care to look after -- to attend to the humanitarian conduct of operations. And furthermore, as I have said, in the commendable documents that outline the doctrine of the Yugoslav army and the discipline of the Yugoslav army, there is also regular reference to the need to conduct military operations with due care to humanitarian and Geneva Conventional issues. And if those directions were followed, then it would be my submission that what I'm purported -- what is purported to have happened there, as described in the indictment, which is the only information I'm dealing with today in terms of what actually happened there, wouldn't have happened. So I must conclude that the doctrine, disciplinary measures, and so on of the Yugoslav army were not adhered to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If what is written in the indictment is correct, right?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: I have made my position with regard to the facts on the ground quite clear. I have the indictment to work on, and that's it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, General. You took an example here. I really don't know how I'm going to fit into this brief period of time that was given to me, because this is very voluminous material. You said a small quantity of documents, and of course documents do exist, because they have to exist. There are documents of the Supreme Command and of the commands of the armies and the commands of the corps and the commands of the brigades. Here in this list, you gave an order issued by a battalion commander. You probably assume, as a soldier, if there is that kind of order at battalion level -- because I see that the signature there is the signature of a major. A major can be a commander of a battalion. Then colonels command brigades in our army. So this was a major. So you may assume that if a battalion commander issues this kind of order, there are orders at brigade level, at corps level, at army level, and that these orders from army level do adhere to orders issued by the Supreme Command. I assume that this is a logical conclusion, because we are not now reconstructing a dinosaur on the basis of a bone from its tail. We are doing this on the basis of an entire body of documents which is tactically only on -- a battalion is only one level above that of company. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: Assuming that your army is constructed on the same line as ours, yes, that is correct and logical, and it would certainly apply generally throughout the world. All I can say in response to what -- the statement you made is this: First of all, I think it is perfectly reasonable to assume that documents would have emanated from the highest level of command in order to generate the dinosaur's tail that you refer to, but all that has been put in front of me has been a dinosaur's tail, that document that I have produced as evidence. And I should add that that was not signed, and without a signature, and without a documentary number, it must put to some question on its validity and authenticity and whether or not it was issued at all. Those are the questions that go through my mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The time has now come to adjourn. Mr. Milosevic, we're going to adjourn, the usual time. Sir Peter, would you be back, please, in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'll just ask the amici this: Are there any questions from the amicus?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and I think it will take about ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you've got, then, about 55 minutes to an hour left.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. May. I shall try to use that. But I do think that that is too short a period of time for such a serious witness. I am saying this because I want it to be on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, did you have the opportunity of seeing the directive of the Supreme Command for the engagement of the army of Yugoslavia? I see that it is marked here, it does have a Prosecution number, and it has been made available. So did you see this directive for the engagement of the army of Yugoslavia in the war in 1999, this directive being issued by the Supreme Command?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: Can anybody refer me to it in my documents?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Which document are you referring to, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm talking about the directive of the Supreme Command for the engagement of the army of Yugoslavia in defence from the NATO aggression in this war. I see that it has a Prosecution number, I see that it has been made available, so I'm asking the witness whether it was made available to him or not. Twelve pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The simplest course: Mr. Nice, do you know what this document is?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't have it at my fingertips and don't know immediately what it is. If the accused is able to produce exhibits in advance and give us notice, we can dig them up and find them, but otherwise, I think he'll just have to make it available to the witness and it will have to go on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, let's see the document, Mr. Milosevic, and then the witness can answer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't have time. I don't have time to look at it now. I'm going to deal with it when its turn comes. KO228612. I asked the general whether he had the opportunity of seeing this directive, directive issued by the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: I don't recollect it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since you also mention in your professional explanations that the Supreme Command issues directives, orders, do you agree with me that this is a document through which a Supreme Command sets tasks for a longer period of time and then commanders of strategic groups are thus in a position to make decisions in the battlefield, according to the principle of unity of command and singleness of command? Is that in keeping with regular procedure in any developed modern army?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: I would say yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is my assertion correct? I'm not a military expert, but as far as I know, not a single directive of Supreme Command in wars waged until now does not not rely upon provisions of humanitarian law, international humanitarian law.

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: Sorry. Could you repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is my assertion correct that not a single directive of a Supreme Command, at least that I know of, in wars waged until now, generally speaking - I'm not referring specifically to the war in Yugoslavia now - does not contain elements that are based on the observance of international humanitarian law?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: I don't have wide enough experience of such directives to comment on the extent that such inferences would be contained in them, but I would say that it is implied, in most civilised and well-structured armies, that application of humanitarian rules of the law should be applied, whether it is put in the documents or whether it isn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm saying that because our directive actually contains that as well. I'm going to quote only one passage to you from page 8. It is marked in the Prosecution case KO228619. And it says: "Towards the enemy, prisoners of war, one should behave in accordance with the Geneva Conventions, international humanitarian law, which is deeply rooted in our national ethos of heroism and fairness as well." So in this directive, in addition to giving instructions and orders to behave in this way, even our national ethos, our national tradition, is referred to. Did you have the opportunity of familiarising yourself with the traditions of warfare of the Serb and Montenegrin peoples, historically speaking, General?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: I did not examine the history of your country. I based my evidence on the documents that were put in front of me, which was, largely speaking, contemporary. However, I would say again that the structure of the army, the doctrine of the army, the legal requirement of the army, all highly commendable and of the highest standard, and the question must surely be: Were they adhered to or were they not?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, by way of clarification, the first of the documents referred to by the accused, and probably the second, I've now tracked down as documents that came into our possession very recently. They were made available post haste to the accused, even, I think, before we had English translations of them, and I think for that reason, or possibly because of the timing of the report, they will not have been shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know, General, that from the point of view of the tradition of the Serb and Montenegrin people, the greatest shame is to shoot at an unarmed man, a civilian, or a prisoner of war?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: That should be the same for my own army, and what one would expect from your army as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know, General, that out of all the former Yugoslavia republics, it is only in the army of Yugoslavia that there is not a single officer and a single general who came to such a position without having all the necessary military skills and without having gone through all the levels that he had to go through in a regular army? And as opposed to other former Yugoslav republics, no political or party leaders, not in a single case, got any command posts or ranks; they did not become generals or anything. The officers of the army are only professionals. So no politicians are there. Did you know about that? Did you see that?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: I have not studied the career structure and history of your senior officers, so I'm not able to comment on that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm talking about all officers, not only senior officers, not only generals, admirals, et cetera. All officers. And could you imagine --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I hesitate to interrupt, but that last question is, in reality, a speech dressed up as a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. It's not a question. Now, this is the way in which time goes and why the accused gets his time limited on each occasion. That, too, should be noted for the record. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. General, can you imagine, as an experienced soldier, that there could be a single professional officer who is duty-bound by his own oath, by the laws that he had to study in all schools and at all levels, and the orders that he was issued; that is to say, duty-bound by everything that he is bound with, including morality and tradition? Can you imagine such an officer ordering the execution of civilians and the execution of prisoners of war and that there could be a unit willing to carry that out in spite of all orders and all documents that are available? Can you imagine that?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: It would be out of place for me to start imagining things, because my evidence is based on the facts and information put in front of me which I've already described. And how individuals behave, particularly when they're under pressure, is a psychological issue which makes an interesting debate. It probably isn't for today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, General. Let's save time. You looked at the principles of command. I'm not going to dwell on that. Duties given to certain individuals, known as the principle of singleness of command, et cetera, and you referred to command in practice. That is page 7. You say: "The supreme military commander and his staff will be in minute-to-minute contact with the field commander and there will be a regular flow of reports, communications, briefings and discussions taking place throughout the battlefield 24 hours a day." Is it clear that this pertains to a field commander; it cannot pertain to the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: The Supreme Command will obviously be working on the basis of one or, at most, two down, as I described in my evidence, and they will need to know, and indeed I would hope professionally will insist on knowing, how the operations are being conducted and what successes and what failures there have been. And as I mentioned earlier, information is the lifeblood of a military machine, and its ability to work effectively in operations that are frequently fast-changing and confused. And if the senior command do not have adequate information made available to them, then they will quickly lose control of their forces. And certainly, on the documents that I've read concerning the structure and command arrangements within the Yugoslav army, and knowing, I'm sure, the competence of senior officers and the training that's gone into them, although I've had no evidence of that, but it would appear that that must have taken place, I would expect them to insist on being kept fully informed of what was going on in the field. It doesn't mean to say that they will know what every section was up to, but they will certainly know the development of events and the pattern of events, which they may or may not wish to influence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, is it logical that our rules provide -- what our rules provided for, the time span for regular information, and when speaking about the time span for regular information, the higher the level, quite understandably, the greater the time interval for information and communication? And on that basis, does it seem to you to be reasonable that the Supreme Command should receive a combat report from the commands of an army once a day, up until a certain hour, every day, except when it requires an extraordinary emergency report, but at least once a day when speaking about the Supreme Command? Is that a reasonable thing? And then going down the chain and to lower levels, it becomes more frequent. And when you get to the tactical level, of course, then there is a permanent insight into the situation and every detail has to be known. Now, is that a reasonable way of information and communication, this kind of flow?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: Without getting involved in a detailed debate on the theory of command, I would go along with that completely. I'm sure there will be variations from time to time, and as you yourself have pointed out. There will be moments when operations are of such an intensity that the senior command will wish to know on a much more immediate basis what is going on. But the operations room of the senior command will in fact be in pretty close and regular touch, bearing in mind the modern communications that are available to a commander these days, with the battlefield. And they will instantly draw the commander's attention to any significant variance or changes or activities that might require his attention at any time of the day or, indeed, the night, for that matter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This directive of the Supreme Command was sent to the strategic groups. The strategic groups in the Yugoslav army, in the VJ, were the 1st army, the 2nd army, the 3rd army, and then we had the air force and anti-air attack units, and the fifth was the navy. Now, is it logical, in view of your profession, that the Supreme Command should know at least what was happening at two levels: The army command level and the corps command level, and that it was permanently informed and kept abreast of that in this daily combat report that was sent in every day and was concluded by a certain hour and minute. Would that be the logical functioning of affairs?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: That would be a perfectly respectable practice, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it clear, when you're talking about coordination, for instance, coordination between the army and the police force, and you mention in that regard the law, and of course there is an order by the Supreme Command on subordination levels, that is to say the police units to the military commander in his area of responsibility. Now, is it clear, General, that we're not dealing here with any kind of subordination of the entire police force to the entire General Staff and all its functions, but it refers to one area of responsibility, whether it is a company, a brigade, a battalion, or whatever, where the fighting is actually going on, that there must be coordination and that it is logical that in situations of that kind, the police group, which is in the area, in the field, should be attached and resubordinated to the military commander so as to avoid mutual killing, confusion, misunderstandings, or anything of that nature?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: You have summarised an ideal situation which I would entirely go along with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you speak about the operations in Kosovo and Metohija, is it clear that the army and the police force communicate with the civilian authorities in the field in that particular locality, but also that, in every respect this is no replacement for the competences of the internal chains of command within the army itself and the police force?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: The army and the police force would maintain the integrity of their own commands, regardless of the arrangements and facilities that were made available for them to cooperate together and perhaps have a joint headquarters or to have liaison officers or radio operators close to their respective headquarters. And I think I made that clear in my evidence, that that would be jealously -- I would expect that to be jealously guarded by, in this case, since this is the issue you've raised, by the police force, and high command in the navy, air force, police units. And in each of those cases, they have always retained a right to refer issues up their own chain of command. And so it behooves a commander to understand the other forces that he is working with - and they all work differently, for a very good reason, which I don't think we want to spend time on today - and to bring them along. And so at a higher level of command, you come into a degree of diplomacy in managing of services. It's not just a situation of, "Do what I say," it's a question of getting them to go along with the overall policy and strategy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it, then, also clear, General, that when we have a joint command of some sort, it's not really a command; it's a horizontal coordination, and that to all practical intents and purposes, all the participants retain their own responsibility and their own chain of command and that an agreement is made only within the frameworks of the competences and authorisations that he has down the chain of his own command?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: Clearly, it depends upon the wording of the command responsibility that is delegated to the commander on the spot, and it may well be that there will be reservations put on it. But let's be quite clear: There's only one man responsible for what goes on on the ground, and that's the boss, and the fact that he's got other people working alongside him or with him does not excuse him from responsibility for what may be going on in the field, whether it's success or whether it is a failure or an abuse of military usage. And if he's got these other people working with him, shall we say for the sake of this discussion from the navy and the army, then they are obliged to carry out the senior commander's requirements. And whilst they do not have the excuse or the privilege or the laxity to work something out on their own because they don't like what the commander says, that is not what I mean when I say they would be able to refer to their own command. If they felt that they were being given orders that were unsuited, resources that they control - so, shall we say, navy and ships, for an example - then it would be perfectly reasonable for them to go back up their own chain of command and to say so, in which case it would go to the central staff and the senior military commander in this example we're discussing would then be questioned and asked to justify what he was trying to do with the navy. But if the military commander is competent, he shouldn't allow the situation to get to that stage of affairs. He should be taking advice and listening. At the end of the day, you listen for so long in military operations and then you make decisions, and they're your decisions and your responsibility and there's no wriggling out of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I completely agree with you. And it is precisely along those lines that I'm commenting what Mr. Nice placed here, put on the ELMO, on the overhead projector here, the page where he quotes you as saying that we should mention that the police force subordinated to the army can be expected to have the right to complain directly to the civilian authorities and police leadership if it considers that it has been abused or that it has been issued orders which are contrary to the law. That is quite logical. But did you have any kind of knowledge that somebody had issued an order which was contrary and in opposition to the law? And when the police or army or whoever was complaining about an order that had been issued, in your work, in the work that you did, did you have any knowledge about anybody issuing any orders which would be contrary and in contravention to the law?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: If you're asking me to pick out instances in my own career of this nature, then clearly this would be possible.
