But I have to say that again, if I may without being too immodest, that one of the reasons why I personally was probably given command in the Gulf was that my experience and my ability to understand the usage of my fellow services was -- had been proven and that this was considered by my responsible superiors, and indeed the government of the day - because I was appointed by the Prime Minister - to be an important aspect, shall we say, of my experience and my character. So I'd like to think I didn't get it too badly wrong. There are cases where people have fallen out, and I'm sure you've read your history and you're probably more competent at it than me, but I don't think that's really relevant to -- I would suggest it's not relevant, Your Honour, to today's discussion, or we're going to devolve into a debate on the ethics of command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But in consideration of your work, you have no knowledge about the fact that in any concrete framework, this framework of war, the war in Yugoslavia in 1999, for instance, that somebody issued any unlawful orders. And of course I completely agree with you that it is the duty of an individual to react to that. That is not being contested, in principle. In principle, that can never be challenged. My question was: Did you actually have any knowledge of anybody issuing an unlawful order and that people failed to react to that perhaps?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: I have been given documents which do not suggest this at all, and one must -- I must therefore make my judgements based on what the indictment says happened on the ground and the way that the military and other forces responded to events.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And is it clear that the representatives of the civilian authorities - for example, in Kosovo, there was the provisional executive government of the province and then there were representatives of the government of Serbia and government of Yugoslavia - is it clear that the representatives of the civilian authorities that communicate both with the military and police authorities do not represent an element in the chain of command, either with the police force or with the army?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: The civilian element was certainly present, on the information that I've been given, and that would seem a commendable arrangement in the senior headquarters down in Kosovo itself. And I don't think I have seen documents that precisely explain what the responsibilities of the individuals on that council were at the time. In fact, I haven't. But I would say that the construction of the local headquarters was right in line with the doctrine of your army and would be something that we could live with ourselves in my army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you happen to know, General, did the information reach you that, for example, that provisional government of Kosovo and Metohija during the war was composed of Serbs, Albanians, Muslims, Turks, Romany, Egyptians, et cetera, and that the Serbs were the minority, even the minority in that provisional government? Do you happen to know about that?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In one place you speak about discipline and discipline is at the basis of morals and ethical standards. That is quite true. Now, do you consider that an army which is not disciplined, not a disciplined army, would succeed in surviving the kind of day-and-night aggression that lasted for 78 days, parallelly with the fighting that went on against the large number -- fighting with the large number of terrorist groups? I'm not going to present maps or facts and figures at this point, ones that were compiled by your own experts as to the distribution of brigades, the operative zones, the terrorist organisations of the KLA, et cetera. But do you consider that an army which was able to survive that kind of aggression and was also simultaneously fighting on the ground could have done so if it had not been a well-disciplined army and that it would have succeeded in protecting the territory, its territory, had it not been disciplined with the minimum losses that it incurred?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to ask the witness if he thinks he can answer that or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'll have a go, Your Honour. I think that the indications are, to me, on the evidence that I'm working off, that the Yugoslav army was disciplined, that it carried out the orders that it was given, and that it behaved in a perfectly respectable way in that respect. The question is: What orders was it given, and what did it do in its interpretation of those orders? This is not to put in question the actual discipline of the army. The discipline of the army, from what I have read, appears to be perfectly satisfactory. So it's a question of what orders it was given on which it acted in a disciplined way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you able to obtain from the opposite party over there any kind of order which would indicate that the army was not instructed, or that an order was issued of any kind which would not be in conformity with the behavior of a modern army engaged in the defence of its country and which was valiantly, at that, defending its own country and adhering to the rules of international warfare and its own rules and regulations? Did you have any knowledge or were you given any material which would point in that direction at all?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: I have limited material, very limited material, on the orders that were issued and the army's and the services' and forces' response to them, and I therefore must judge, using the indictment, which is the only indication I have as to what happened on -- official indication I have as to what happened on the ground, as my marker as to what the army and the services did and how they conducted it. Now, what orders were actually issued - and to be quite clear, it may be verbal, it may be written orders - in order to initiate those events, I have not had access to. May I add something, Your Honour? I think it is important in this issue of discipline to understand that I felt that the Yugoslav army was disciplined, and one must therefore discount the fact that what they did there was that of an ill-disciplined, self -- independently-motivated rebel. It wasn't; it was a coordinated operation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Without a doubt, a disciplined army, therefore, which was able to survive all that, it would be difficult to be able to accuse that kind of army of having perpetrated the kinds of things that it has been -- that have been held up here and accused of doing here. But to avoid any lack of clarity, when you look at the exaggerated behaviour, and because of the possible abuse of interpretation, I should like to clarify one particular point and issue. What is referred to is that it is possible that the lower-down commanders, less-senior commanders, made errors for which the higher-up commanders were not aware of, that they might have made erroneous assessments, et cetera. I hope that you're not saying that anybody in the structure of the Yugoslav army presented this kind of assertion as being a justification.

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: I would concur with your suggestion that in any warfare - and I'm sure this was no exception - there will be commanders who fail to meet up to expectations for whatever reasons, and I've covered that in my report. The question is, though: If that is the case, and they broke the regulations of the Yugoslav army, why was no significant disciplinary and investigatory inquiry set up to look into these cases which you're suggesting might have happened? And I have to come back, Your Honour, to the matter that the events that we are discussing and which the whole of my evidence is based were so widespread, so coordinated, involving so much territory and so many people, in order to administer them just logistically, quite apart from any military thing, that we are well beyond the odd commander diverging from the strict instructions that he was given.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, that's precisely what I wish to stress. I hope that - and I'm claiming that no higher-up commander, no senior commander, not a single one, from brigade commander level right up to me as the Supreme Commander, did not in that respect use any justification and say that it was -- that what was done was done by the lower-down commanders that were going against the grain of the law or acting contrary to the orders he received, that they were disobedient, and this would have been a shameful -- that is to say, if the superior commanders were to justify themselves by any errors committed on the part of the lower-down officers, and I want to refute that kind of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You're not giving evidence now, as you know. Now, what is your question for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I think that I have clarified the question. So you, General, consider that what was the subject of your attention could have occurred only if everything was well organised down the vertical chain of command, that the only fact -- and the only fact that I'm drawing your attention to is the following: That what the indictment is claiming is not true, is false, and not that it is an error on the part of somebody at a lower level but that the indictment is a false one. That is what I am claiming, and you quite obviously do not have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we've had this argument. Now, have you any more questions?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course I do, yes. Just let me look at my notes. Mr. May, as you asked me about my question, and questions, I'm talking about this excessive behaviour, and where the general speaks about it, and I can't support any assertion where it says that the events described in the indictment, et cetera, are the result of erroneous assessments brought in by the lower-level commands. So we're talking about that same issue, the same point, that in proving the correctness of the indictment, you are using the indictment itself. The indictment is being used as a purpose unto itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... questions which are not repetitious and are relevant, I'm going to ask Mr. Wladimiroff to start.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 26, perhaps that's the right page - I do have a little time, Mr. May - you state that the law on the Yugoslav army is a well-formulated, commendable one which every nation could be proud of if it were to be translated into the legal behaviour of its armed forces. Now, can you, General, assume, at least in an analysis of this kind, that that is so and that the armed forces did in fact behave in conformity with the law and not in conformity with the indictment?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: I can make no such assumption.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have several more questions. In preparing yourself, did you come across any documentation on the words of illegal financing and arming terrorist groups of the KLA from Germany, Switzerland, the United States, and from your own country? Did you come across any information and documentation pertaining to that?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: None at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you consider that in this expert report, one can exclude a series of facts, like the very NATO aggression itself, without speaking of the sanctions that came before it and the hostile attitude to Serbia? In an expert report of this kind, can you exclude such factors?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: I can only make my judgement on the evidence that has been presented to me and which you have full access to, and then linking that to my own experience, and that is what I've done. And where there may be any deficiencies in what I have to say, it is because I didn't have the facts put in front of me, if they existed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Quite specifically: For example, the existence of a large number of orders on compulsory observance of the provisions of international law. Why do you interpret that as a reflection of a lack of observance of these principles and you preclude the more logical assumption that the situation became increasingly difficult for officers and soldiers under round-the-clock bombing? And then on the other hand, there was close cooperation with the KLA, who were aided by the other sided? That is one element. And another element is that a comprehensive order from headquarters, the Supreme Command, was codification of many orders, which is, after all, customary in the army, in the military. When there are several orders that are issued, they may all fall within a single one in order to lend themselves to practical use. So why do you interpret this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I've completely lost the thread of this. What are you putting to the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the general spoke about this. I'm sure he understands me. And if he doesn't, I'll repeat the question for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. You must make the questions plain, instead of a rambling speech. Now, come on. Make it plain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you understand me, General?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Mr. Milosevic, you are to ask the question again. Now, put it again. You're being instructed to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You made an observation about the existence of a large number of orders on the compulsory observance of provisions of international law and the law of war; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: I'd be grateful if you'd refer me to the part in my text that you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My papers are quite chaotic now, there are so many of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, perhaps you could help with the reference. Certainly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it related to footnote 11?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think it's on page 20 probably. And you'll find it, at least in the English version --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Nice, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry. I think you'll find it on page 20. It's maybe what the accused is referring to. It's, in any event, a sentence beginning: "I have read the translation of the book ..."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've lost the translation here. I think there's an electronic fault.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. de la Billiere, the last paragraph on page 20: "[In English] In this I note that between mid-1998 and June 1999, there was an extensive range of orders issued from the Supreme Command staff down to at least corps level, emphasising the VJ's concern to abide by international humanitarian regulation concerning the conduct of war. I was somewhat surprised at the volume of orders and the need for them to be reiterated at regular intervals." [Interpretation] My question was why the existence of a large number of documents that you refer to, you understand to be perhaps an expression of a lack of respect for these orders, why do you preclude a more logical possibility, that there is a growing challenge, things became increasingly difficult for soldiers and officers with round-the-clock bombing and constant clashes with the KLA? That is one element. And another element is that after several orders, like in any other army, they're all subsumed in one. Aren't these explanations more logical to you than the ones that I quoted to you just now?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: I understand what you're getting at. First of all, a lot of these were not orders; they were in the document which was produced after the war, I believe, the book which has been made -- introduced as evidence during today's hearing. And there was in that a continual repetition of the -- emphasising that the military command felt it necessary to keep continually repeating the need to adhere to the humanitarian and Geneva Convention aspects of war. And as I mentioned earlier, in a previous question you raised, I felt that these issues, first of all, in a well-disciplined, well-trained army, would be normal and common practice and not need continually emphasising. Secondly, the book, of course, is not an issuing of orders, it was a regurgitation of events, and we must remember that. It's not an executive document in itself. And I still adhere to that. It's very commendable that the Yugoslav army should wish to and should expect to adhere to these humanitarian requirements and the Geneva Convention. But I have to ask myself why it's necessary to go on repeating it when it is part of their ethos and their doctrine, as stated in other standard procedures produced to me; for instance, the law of the army itself, which extensively emphasises the need for this. So why should the need be felt to continually repeat this particular aspect of the orders issued within the chain of command?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that's precisely what I asked you. Why do you preclude the more logical possibility of greater stress and pressure which is becoming overwhelming for officers and soldiers, given day-to-day fighting and round-the-clock bombing? And isn't it logical to emphasise that time and again that this has to be abided by? You also say that you did not see orders, but there are orders of the commander of the Pristina corps that date back to 1998, pertaining to Kosovo specifically, and that has to do with honouring these rules, although there was no external aggression then, although terrorists do not fall under the Geneva Convention, but we did treat them as if they did because we wanted it to be quite clear. And this was as far back as 1998. Did you have that order in your hands perhaps?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: I'm not sure which order you're referring to, but I would confirm that there was a continual repetition of the need to maintain humanitarian practices and to adhere to the Geneva Convention, and in the documents that I've seen, this has been continually emphasised. And so one would ask oneself: Why is it continually emphasised? Because normally in the military chain of command you don't need to go on emphasising. It's part of the practice and doctrine of a well-structured army, and indeed it is part of the practice and doctrine of your army, and therefore presumably your officers and soldiers have been trained and made aware of these practices from very early in their careers and it is part of their life. If they are conforming to them, then that is fine. But if they're not conforming to them - and the evidence that I'm basing my statement on implies that they were not - why was it felt necessary for the chain of command to continually repeat the need to conform to them and subsequently, of course, to produce this book which particularly emphasised these issues?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The book was issued later. But tell me: When you say "evidence," are you referring to the allegations contained in the indictment?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: My entire statement is based on the indictment as it stands today. It does not assume that it is proven, it assumes that that is the basis on which I have been asked to make my comments to the Court. And as I said earlier on, if the indictment is incorrect or if it is not fully proven, then my comments will have to be taken into account with that additional evidence. And I don't think that I have anything more to say beyond the fact that that's where my comments have stemmed from. And it's not for me to comment on the correctness or otherwise of the indictment itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have said enough, General. After all, if somebody breaks a compass and then you take all necessary action to go north and you are moving south, nevertheless you will sweat. I have another question. The relationship between the military and economic powers that attacked Yugoslavia, has this -- have you been compelled to look only at the relationship between the army and the KLA due to that?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: I have not been tasked with discussing the relationships between the military and the economic powers that you say attacked Yugoslavia. That is not part of my limit, and I have nothing to say on that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can one have a comprehensive assessment, even of this purely military aspect, if one does not look at the NATO aggression and other pressures, and if it is all reduced to the relationship between the army and the police, on the one hand, and the KLA, on the other hand? Is it then possible to carry out a comprehensive and objective analysis?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: I think others must be the judge of whether the analysis that I have made, based on the evidence that I have given to the Court and the assumptions that I've made before the Court, is comprehensive enough or not. That's where it comes from, and I'm afraid we can't change that today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, your time is almost up. That is a point which you have made before. Now you can ask two more questions, if you need to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does this also put forth a reservation in relation to what you used from the indictment? You talk about large-scale killings, et cetera, large-scale killings like Racak. Now there's another one, Izbica, et cetera. Do you know that none of these so-called large-scale killings has been proven? And do you have any idea --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, Mr. Milosevic. We're just wasting time going over the same point quite endlessly. It's not for the witness to comment on these matters. It's a matter which we will have to decide. Mr. Wladimiroff.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Questioned by Mr. Wladimiroff:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, at your time, you were a man of the troops, rather than a desk officer, were you not?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: I had spent a limited amount of my time in my service sitting behind a desk. Most of my time was in command, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From your resume, it seems you mainly served within the British army rather than in an international function, as for example, NATO function, commanding troops of various nations; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: No, I don't think it is, with respect. I -- obviously, I was part of the British army for my entire career, wherever I was serving, but I spent more time than most people on what we call loan service, that's attachment from the British army to other armies. And the two notable things in the -- what is now the southern Yemen in Aden, where I spent two years attached to the Jashale jihad [phoen], which is Arabic for the federal army of Aden, which is an Arab army, and then I spent two years, approximately, attached to the Sudanese army. And in that respect I therefore spent four years totally separated from the British army's activities and understanding and working with, under command of, a foreign army. There are, of course, many other situations where I have worked alongside foreign armies, and I don't think we need to go into all of that; it's there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Certainly not. These secondments were in 1995 and 1983; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: By these "secondments," you mean these attachments.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sudan and --

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: Sudan --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- and the Arab army.

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: Yes. They were two years. Aden was in 1983. I was --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The other one was in 1955.

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: Sorry. I've lost communications again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever command a foreign army --

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: No. I'm sorry. That is not correct. I was in Sudan in the late 1970s, approximately 1978 to 1980, not 1955.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Did you ever command a foreign army or foreign troops, except for these two secondments, that is, Sudan and, let's say, Yemen?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: Without going again through a rather long career, let me take the latest events, shall we say, the Gulf War, and in the Gulf War, I certainly had under my authority troops from foreign armies. I can't, off the top of my head, tell you exactly who they were, but I could give you two or three, if you really wanted them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. Thank you. Now, if one makes a distinction between general observations and specific observations, am I right in thinking when I assume that your expertise relates to the principles and the mechanism of armies, their structure and functions? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: Yes, it is. I mean, inevitably, if I worked and served in foreign armies, I would have to understand their principles and their structure and their functions in order to do my job.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. On the basis of that expertise related to the principles and mechanism of armies, their structure and functions, you make your general observations; is that right, in your report?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: I make my observations within my report on the basis of my entire career, of which these are specific occasions or periods.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in these general observations, you set out the norms as you experienced them through your career; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure what you mean by "norms." Could you be kind enough to just clarify that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we make a distinction between general observations, what a regular proper army could do, and specific observations that are related to the VJ, I refer you to your general observations, and I take it - at least, I think that's right - that your general observations reflect what you think is right on the basis of your experience throughout your career.

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: Clearly, that is correct so far as it goes. But we must be quite clear that in making any comments about the VJ, I have applied my -- the experience of my career to the documents that have been presented to me on the structure and the doctrine of the VJ army, and I have already said that I thought they were commendable documents and ones that --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We will come to that. We will come to that. Am I also right in thinking that your specific observations are based on the documents you have reviewed? And with "specific observations," I mean your observations on the VJ and the police.

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Would you also agree that what has been presented to you and the documents you reviewed were a selection of what you could have seen if you had full access to the original documents?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: I don't know what original documents were available, and I did not see, so I don't think I can answer that accurately. What I would say is this, though: That I thought there was a dearth of documents and documentary evidence covering the period of conflict that we are looking at, and I do have to ask myself why this is so, where it has gone, and why an organised and disciplined army, such as the VJ army, if they didn't actually have those documents at all, why were they diverging so widely from their own doctrine and their own regulations? If, on the other hand, they did exist, then I would like to have seen them, but they weren't presented to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would appreciate a little bit shorter answers, General, if you please. Do you have the impression that you've not seen all available documents, and therefore you appreciate you have seen a selection only?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: I think I've said previously that I am surprised there are not more documents available.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: I have no reason -- I have no knowledge as to why there are not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Am I right in thinking that the meaning of your report is merely setting the standards and basis of your experience, rather than making judgements on the basis of full access to all the information available to the actions of the VJ in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: I said at the beginning of my evidence that I am not an expert on what happened in Kosovo, and so clearly my experience is what is being brought to bear here and I would support what you say in principle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Would you agree that writing an opinion on an issue one researches, by all reasonable standards would require an acknowledgment of all the sources of the author? Please answer with yes or no.

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: I would -- I'm not sure where this applies to my -- specifically to my evidence. I would have expected to have had put in front of me such documentary evidence as was available. If stuff was available and it was not put in front of me, then clearly I do not have the benefit of that when making my judgements.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you consider to acknowledge all the sources as an attachment to your report by way of a list of sources you have reviewed?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: You're really questioning me now on the conduct of the Court, which I don't think I'm competent to comment on. I've listed what I had access to, and you know that, and that's been presented to the Court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I can only understand what you have reviewed by reading your report. In there, there are some references and there are footnotes, and that's all we have. So am I right in thinking, then, that all the sources are limited to your references in your report and the footnotes, or is there anything more you have seen we don't know?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: There is nothing that I have seen in the context of this case that I have not referred to, so far as I am aware. And perhaps I could ask my learned friend on my right to comment on that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I take it that if you express an opinion, a specific opinion, on the VJ, on the MUP, in Kosovo, the source must be found in your report, either in the report itself or in the footnote, because that's what you're saying, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. So if I give you some examples, on page 2 --

utterances.speaker: PETER DE LA BILLIERE
utterances.text: Page 2 of my evidence?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Page 2 of your report. Under the heading of Command and Control, where you say, in the third line: "According to the documentation I've read ..." It must be your documentation as you just gave evidence about which is referred to in your report or a footnote. And the same goes for page 9, first fresh paragraph, line 4: "From the information I've read ..." And so on on page 14, first fresh paragraph: "According to the documents I have reviewed ..." Page 19, the last paragraph: "From the information I have reviewed ..." Page 20 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Wladimiroff, I see there's a reference there to the OTP military analyst's report, that one. Now, we are trespassing on the time of the next hearing. If possible, we should finish the witness so that he can get away. Now, what is the position? You said ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes, but the answers were a little bit longer than I expected, to be true. I'm afraid I'm not able to do this in a very short period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is the position, Mr. Nice?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Two positions, really: First of all, as to the witness, I suspect the witness will make himself available, but it's inconvenient. Secondly, I'm not really quite sure where this line of cross-examination is taking us, in any event, given the attitude of the accused in relation to the evidence of the witness, much of which he's actually accepted, the margin being elsewhere. And as to any criticism there may be of the report, if that's what Mr. Wladimiroff is getting at, Your Honour has already identified that a great deal of material was available to the witness through the report of Mr. Coo, a great deal of evidence in that way. And so unless he's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, the amicus is entitled to cross-examine. I'm not anxious to stop him. But, Sir Peter, we are in this difficulty; that we have to leave this courtroom because another case needs it, and Mr. Wladimiroff has some more questions. Can you make yourself available tomorrow, or is it going to be very inconvenient?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, it's inconvenient, but I think it's more important that the requirements of the Court are met. We haven't all put the time and effort into this to just meet lesser important engagements, and I can be available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, the Court is grateful.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I apologise for this inconvenience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, Mr. Wladimiroff, there's no need to apologise. We'll adjourn now. 9.00 tomorrow morning. We will conclude this evidence before going on to anything else. Apologies to the next case. Perhaps the registry would pass that on.
